topicNames.IV.6: Tax Treatment of Insurance Premiums, Proceeds, and Dividends

items.stem: Why do permanent life policies, such as whole life, tend to cost more than term policies for the same face amount?
options: They include a savings element that builds cash value
They pay a death benefit for a set number of years
They are exempt from state premium taxes
They require a medical exam each year
items.explanation: Per NJ DOBI, Consumer Information: Life Insurance, permanent insurance includes a savings element, so its premiums tend to be higher than term insurance premiums.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a form of permanent life insurance?
options: Whole life
Universal life
Level term
Variable universal life
items.explanation: Per NJ DOBI, Consumer Information: Life Insurance, universal life, variable universal life and whole life are permanent insurance. Term insurance covers only a set term.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the premiums on a traditional whole life policy?
options: They rise each time the policy renews
They can be skipped whenever the cash value is large enough
They are set by the policyowner each year
They stay level for as long as the insured lives
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, whole life covers the insured for life if premiums are paid, and the premium is generally the same for as long as the insured lives.

items.stem: A client compares a 20-pay whole life policy with an ordinary (continuous-premium) whole life policy of the same face amount, issued at the same age. The 20-pay policy's annual premium will be:
options: Higher, since premiums are paid over fewer years
Lower, since coverage ends after 20 years
The same, since the face amounts match
Lower at first, then higher after year 10
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, whole life policies that let you pay premiums for a shorter period, such as 20 years or until age 65, carry higher premiums because payments are made over a shorter period.

items.stem: A 35-year-old plans to keep $250,000 of coverage until age 85. Compared with buying whole life now, renewing annual term the whole time would most likely mean:
options: Higher premiums at first, but lower premiums in later years
Lower premiums at first, but much higher premiums in later years
The same total premiums, paid on a different schedule
Lower premiums throughout, with the same cash value
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, whole life premiums start higher than term premiums but are smaller than the premiums you would eventually pay if you kept renewing term into your later years.

items.stem: Which type of life insurance has a cash value that changes with the performance of investment options the owner picks from a menu, typically mutual funds?
options: Variable life
Universal life
Whole life
Indexed universal life
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Variable Life Insurance guide, variable life has a cash value that varies with the performance of investment options the owner chooses, typically mutual funds. Universal life credits interest, indexed universal life ties crediting to an index, and whole life has guaranteed values.

items.stem: If the investment options a variable life policyowner selects perform poorly, the owner:
options: Keeps a guaranteed minimum cash value
Receives a refund of premiums from the insurer
Can lose earnings, but not the initial investment
Could lose money, including the initial investment
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Variable Life Insurance guide, a variable life policyowner can lose money, including the initial investment, if the chosen investment options perform poorly.

items.stem: Which feature most sets universal life apart from traditional whole life?
options: The cash value is tied to separate investment accounts
The premium is guaranteed level for life
The owner can vary premium payments and adjust the face amount
It covers the insured for a set term of years
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, universal life is a flexible policy that lets the owner vary premium payments and adjust the face amount. Increases may require proof of insurability.

items.stem: A universal life owner has paid very small premiums for several years, and the interest credited plus her payments have not covered the policy's charges. If this continues, what will happen?
options: The insurer will switch the policy to term at the same premium
The face amount will rise to match the charges
The charges will be waived until interest rates recover
The account value will keep falling until coverage ends
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, when universal life premiums plus interest are less than the charges, the account value falls, and if it keeps dropping, coverage eventually ends.

items.stem: A variable universal life owner skips premiums for several years while her subaccounts perform poorly and she carries a policy loan. What is the main risk?
options: The account runs dry and the coverage ends with nothing paid
The insurer bills her for all missed premiums plus interest
The death benefit drops to the total premiums she paid
The policy becomes a modified endowment contract
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor.gov: Variable Life Insurance, a policy may lapse without value if the cash value cannot pay its fees and expenses, which can result from fees, poor investment performance or loans.

items.stem: A variable universal life policy has a $250,000 face amount and $40,000 of cash value. The owner chose the death benefit option equal to the face amount plus the cash value. If the insured dies now, the death benefit is:
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor.gov: Variable Life Insurance, one death benefit option equals the face amount plus the cash value: $250,000 plus $40,000 is $290,000.

items.stem: A level death benefit universal life policy has a $500,000 face amount and $120,000 of cash value. What is the insurer's net amount at risk?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor.gov: Variable Life Insurance, net amount at risk is the difference between the face amount and the cash value: $500,000 minus $120,000 is $380,000.

items.stem: Which is a typical effect of taking a policy loan from a variable life policy?
options: It is taxed as ordinary income when taken
It triggers a surrender charge
It lowers the cash value and makes lapse more likely
It increases the death benefit by the loan amount
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor.gov: Variable Life Insurance, policy loans typically reduce the cash value, increasing the likelihood of lapse, may reduce the death benefit, are typically not subject to surrender charges, and are taken without paying federal taxes.

items.stem: A client buys a standard 20-year level term life policy at age 40 and is still alive when the term ends at age 60. What does the policy pay?
options: The face amount, as a living benefit
The cash value built up over 20 years
A refund of all premiums paid
Nothing, because no death occurred during the term
items.explanation: Per NJ DOBI, Consumer Information: Life Insurance, term insurance pays a death benefit only if the insured dies during the term, and it does not build cash value.

items.stem: Compared with permanent life insurance, term insurance generally has:
options: Lower early premiums and no cash value
Higher early premiums and a growing cash value
Lower early premiums and a guaranteed cash value
Higher early premiums and no cash value
items.explanation: Per NJ DOBI, Consumer Information: Life Insurance, term insurance generally has lower premiums in the early years and does not build up cash values.

items.stem: A client's renewable 10-year term policy is ending, and she has developed heart disease since buying it. If she renews for another term, she can expect:
options: Coverage to continue, likely at a higher premium
To be declined, because her health has changed
To keep the same premium as her first term
To have the face amount reduced to her cash value
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, most term policies can be renewed for one or more terms even if health has changed, and premiums may be higher at each renewal.

items.stem: A client with a convertible term policy has been diagnosed with diabetes and wants permanent coverage. Within the conversion period, he can generally:
options: Convert it if he first passes a medical exam
Exchange it for a cash value policy without proving good health
Convert it, keeping the same premium he pays for term
Exchange it for a policy with a higher face amount at term rates
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, many term policies can be traded for a cash value policy during a conversion period even if the insured is not in good health, though the new premium will be higher than the term premium.

items.stem: A young parent on a tight budget needs the largest possible death benefit for the next 20 years. Which type of policy generally provides the most coverage per premium dollar?
options: Whole life
Universal life
Term life
Variable life
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, term insurance generally offers the largest insurance protection for your premium dollar.

items.stem: A re-entry term policy lets the insured requalify for lower rates at the end of the level period by taking a new policy at current rates. Under New Jersey rules, the new policy:
options: Is a continuation of the old policy, with no new contestable period
May be contested only as to the premium difference
Cannot require any new evidence of insurability
Is treated as a replacement, and the whole contract may be contestable for two years
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.11(a)5-6 provides that if requalification requires issuing a new policy at current rates, the entire contract may be contestable for up to two years, and the transaction is a replacement subject to N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.

items.stem: At age 70, Dana buys an annuity with one lump-sum payment, and her monthly income checks begin a few weeks later. Dana bought:
options: A deferred annuity
An immediate annuity
A variable life policy
A registered index-linked annuity
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, an immediate annuity is bought with a single payment and income typically begins within one year of purchase.

items.stem: During the accumulation phase, what does a fixed deferred annuity guarantee?
options: Its current interest rate for the life of the contract
Returns tied to a stock index
Withdrawals free of surrender charges
A floor on credited interest
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, fixed annuities guarantee at least a minimum interest rate. They may credit more, but only the minimum is guaranteed.

items.stem: Which type of deferred annuity can credit negative interest, reducing contract value, when its benchmark index performs poorly?
options: Fixed annuity
Registered index-linked annuity (RILA)
Fixed indexed annuity
Immediate annuity
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, a RILA can credit negative interest when the index performs poorly, so the owner can lose money. A fixed indexed annuity's credited interest never falls below zero.

items.stem: Which type of annuity lets the owner direct contributions among a menu of mutual funds, with no limit on gains or losses?
options: Fixed annuity
Fixed indexed annuity
Variable annuity
Registered index-linked annuity
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, variable annuities let the owner direct contributions to a menu of mutual funds, with no limits on losses or gains.

items.stem: Of the four main types of deferred annuities, which two are securities that must register with the SEC?
options: Fixed annuities and fixed indexed annuities
Fixed annuities and RILAs
Fixed indexed annuities and variable annuities
RILAs and variable annuities
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, RILAs and variable annuities are securities that must register with the SEC. Fixed and fixed indexed annuities are insurance products regulated by the states.

items.stem: An owner of a registered MVA annuity withdraws money before the end of the specified interest period. What can the insurer do?
options: Change the contract's value, often reducing it
Pay a higher fixed rate for the rest of the period
Convert the contract into an index-linked annuity
Waive any charges, since the rate was fixed
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, a registered MVA annuity pays a fixed rate over a specified period but may adjust the contract value, often down, if money is withdrawn early.

items.stem: The guarantees in an annuity contract are backed primarily by:
options: FDIC deposit insurance
The issuing insurer's claims-paying ability
The SEC's investor protection fund
The performance of a stock index
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, an insurer's obligations under an annuity are subject to its financial strength and claims-paying ability. Annuities are not FDIC-insured.

items.stem: Which feature do annuities generally provide before income payments begin?
options: Deferral of tax on earnings
Tax-free withdrawals at any age
FDIC insurance on the account value
A guaranteed return above market rates
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, annuities provide tax-deferred growth until income payments begin.

items.stem: In a registered index-linked annuity (RILA), the insurer generally sets parameters that:
options: Limit gains but guarantee no losses
Limit losses but allow unlimited gains
Lock in a minimum fixed interest rate
Limit both gains and losses
items.explanation: Per the SEC, Investor.gov: Annuities guide, the insurer generally sets RILA parameters that limit both gains and losses.

items.stem: An indexed annuity has an 80% participation rate and no cap or spread. The index gains 10% over the measuring period. What is credited?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, the participation rate sets how much of the index gain is credited. Eighty percent of 10% is 8%.

items.stem: A client's indexed annuity carries a 6% rate cap. The linked index rises 11% this crediting period, and there is no participation limit or spread. What is credited?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, a rate cap is the maximum positive return the contract can earn, so an 11% index gain is credited at the 6% cap.

items.stem: An indexed annuity has a 2.5% spread and no cap or participation limit. The index gains 8%. What is credited?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, a spread subtracts a set percentage from any gain in the index: 8% minus 2.5% is 5.5%.

items.stem: An indexed annuity has a 50% participation rate and a 1% spread. The participation rate is applied to the index gain first, and then the spread is subtracted. The index gains 12%. What is credited?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, combined features are applied in sequence: 12% times 50% is 6%, minus the 1% spread is 5%.

items.stem: An index reports a 9% total return for the year, of which 2% came from dividends. Under a typical indexed annuity, the index gain used to calculate the credit is:
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, index gains are generally calculated without dividends, so 9% minus 2% of dividends leaves 7% before any participation rate, cap or spread.

items.stem: An index-linked annuity has a 10% buffer. The index falls 15% in the period. Before any surrender charges, how much does the contract value lose?
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, a buffer absorbs a set percentage of loss first. A 15% drop minus the 10% buffer leaves a 5% loss. A 10% floor would instead cap the loss at 10%.

items.stem: Which index-linked annuity feature caps the owner's loss at a set maximum percentage, with the insurer absorbing any decline beyond that point?
options: A buffer
A rate cap
A participation rate
A floor
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, a floor limits exposure to a set percentage of potential loss. A buffer instead absorbs the first set percentage of loss, and the owner bears the rest.

items.stem: A client bought an indexed annuity with a 7% cap. Two years later the cap for the new period is 5%. Is this typical?
options: No, a cap is locked in at issue for the whole contract
No, the participation rate may change but the cap may not
Yes, but a new cap has to be higher than the old one
Yes, insurers commonly reset caps from period to period
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor Bulletin: Indexed Annuities, indexed annuity contracts commonly allow the insurer to change some features periodically, such as the rate cap.

items.stem: A retiree annuitized her variable annuity last year and now receives monthly income. She wants to take out a lump sum for a home repair. In general:
options: She can withdraw from the account at any time
She can withdraw up to 10% per year without penalty
She cannot withdraw from the account once payments have begun
She can withdraw after the surrender period ends
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor.gov: Variable Annuities, annuities generally do not allow withdrawals from the account once income payments have started.

items.stem: A variable annuity owner paid in $100,000, took no withdrawals, and dies during the accumulation phase when the account is worth $82,000. The contract has a common standard death benefit. The beneficiary most likely receives:
items.explanation: Per the SEC Investor.gov: Variable Annuities, a common death benefit pays the greater of the account value or a guaranteed minimum such as purchase payments minus prior withdrawals. The greater of $82,000 and $100,000 is $100,000.

items.stem: A client wants an immediate annuity but asks to pay for it in 12 monthly installments. Under New Jersey rules:
options: Not allowed; it has to be bought with one payment
Allowed, if all payments finish within 12 months
Allowed, if the first payment is at least half
Not allowed, unless the annuitant is over 65
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-43.4(b) requires the premium for an immediate annuity to be paid in a lump sum, not funded on an installment basis. A client who wants to pay over time would use a deferred annuity.

items.stem: Under New Jersey's individual annuity form standards, may one contract form be issued as both an immediate annuity and a deferred annuity?
options: Yes, if the owner elects at issue
No, the same form may not be used for both
Yes, if the insurer files both versions
No, unless it is a variable annuity
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-43.3(c)3 bars issuing the same contract form as both an immediate and a deferred annuity.

items.stem: A married couple buys one joint life policy that pays as soon as either spouse dies. This is a:
options: Second-to-die policy
First-to-die policy
Family income policy
Modified whole life policy
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, a first-to-die policy pays a death benefit when the first insured person dies.

items.stem: A wealthy married couple wants a policy whose proceeds will arrive when estate taxes come due, after both of them have died. Which policy fits best?
options: First-to-die
Decreasing term
Second-to-die
Credit life
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, a second-to-die policy pays when the last insured dies and is often bought by married couples to protect assets from federal estate taxes.

items.stem: Eight months after a second-to-die policy is issued on a married couple, one spouse dies by suicide. The form does not elect to continue the survivorship contract. Under New Jersey rules, the insurer must:
options: Reissue it as single-life coverage on the survivor, with no new evidence
Rescind the whole policy and refund every premium paid
Pay the full face amount now, as if both had died
Keep the survivorship policy but double the premium
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.10(c)1-2 requires the insurer, when only the first insured to die commits suicide in the first two years, to reform and reissue the contract as a single-life policy on the survivor as of the original effective date, without evidence of insurability. Rescission is allowed only if both insureds or the surviving insured commit suicide in that period. The insurer may instead continue the survivorship contract.

items.stem: New Jersey's required 2-year incontestable provision does NOT have to apply to which part of a life policy?
options: The base death benefit
The beneficiary designation
The policy loan provision
An accidental death and dismemberment rider
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-4 excludes provisions on disability benefits and on additional benefits for accidental death, dismemberment or loss of sight from the incontestable requirement.

items.stem: An insured becomes disabled by a condition named in a rider. The policy stays in force, and the owner owes nothing to the insurer while the disability lasts. Which rider is at work?
options: Accidental death benefit rider
Guaranteed insurability rider
Long-term care rider
Waiver of premium rider
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, a waiver of premium rider lets you stop paying premiums if you develop a covered illness or disability named in the rider.

items.stem: A $100,000 policy has a double indemnity rider. The insured dies in a car accident that the rider covers. The beneficiary receives:
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, an accidental death benefit rider, sometimes called double or triple indemnity, pays a multiple of the death benefit for covered accidents. Double indemnity on $100,000 pays $200,000.

items.stem: A client with a guaranteed insurability rider develops a serious illness, then reaches one of the rider's option dates and buys more coverage. The premium for the added coverage is based on:
options: How old he is and how much coverage he adds
His current health and medical history
The premium rate set when the policy was issued
A medical exam taken on the option date
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, a guaranteed insurability rider allows increases at set times without a medical exam, and the cost depends on age and the amount of the increase, not health or lifestyle.

items.stem: A long-term care rider on a life policy usually pays out when the insured:
options: Is diagnosed with any illness that shortens life expectancy
Needs help with basic tasks such as bathing or dressing
Retires and stops earning income
Reaches the policy's maturity age
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, a long-term care rider lets the insured use part of the death benefit for long-term care, and usually requires being unable to do certain activities of daily living.

items.stem: A terminally ill insured receives an accelerated death benefit and wants to use it for a family trip. Under a typical accelerated benefit rider, this is:
options: Not allowed, since the money is reserved for medical bills
Allowed, but limited to nursing home costs
Allowed, since the money need not go toward care
Not allowed until the beneficiary consents
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, an accelerated death benefit lets a terminally ill insured take money from the death benefit, and the money does not have to be used for care related to the illness.

items.stem: If a rider attached to a life policy conflicts with one of the policy's original provisions, which controls?
options: The original policy provision
Whichever favors the insurer
The application
The rider
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, a rider is a written agreement that adds, subtracts or modifies coverage, and it takes precedence over the original provisions of the policy.

items.stem: A family rider added to a parent's life policy usually provides what kind of coverage on the other family members?
options: Term insurance
Whole life insurance
Variable life insurance
Universal life insurance
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, a family rider allows term insurance on all or certain family members under the policy.

items.stem: A 25-year-old with a strong family history of heart disease can afford only a small policy now but expects to need much more coverage later. Which rider best protects his ability to buy that coverage?
options: Waiver of premium
Guaranteed insurability
Accidental death benefit
Family term
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, the guaranteed insurability option allows buying more death benefit at stated times without evidence of insurability, which may help someone with a family history of significant medical problems and limited current income.

items.stem: A parent's life policy includes a rider covering the parent's spouse. The rider says the spouse's coverage ends when the parent dies. The parent dies midway through a paid premium period. Under New Jersey rules, the policy must:
options: Refund the unearned premium, or keep the coverage for the paid period
Pay the spouse's face amount to the estate right away
Convert the spouse coverage to whole life automatically
End the spouse coverage at once, with no refund at all
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.9(a)1-3 requires a form that ends other-insured coverage at the primary insured's death to return the unearned premium, or else continue the coverage for the remainder of the period paid for.

items.stem: Under New Jersey rules, which is one permitted way for a policy to keep a child rider in force after the primary insured parent dies?
options: Waiving the premium for the child coverage
Raising the child coverage to the parent's face amount
Requiring the child to prove insurability again
Paying the child coverage's face amount to the estate
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.9(a)1-3 permits a form to continue coverage on the other insured by waiver of premium, or by other permitted methods such as paid-up term.

items.stem: An annuity has a nursing home waiver of surrender charges. The contract names no other family members. Whose nursing home confinement would qualify for the waiver under New Jersey rules?
options: The owner's adult daughter
The owner's brother
The annuitant's spouse
The annuitant's parent
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-43.6 limits the nursing home waiver to confinement of the owner, the annuitant, or the owner's or annuitant's spouse or civil union partner. Other family members do not qualify.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, the grace period for premiums after the first on an ordinary individual life policy must be at least:
options: 10 days
28 days
30 days
60 days
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-3 requires a grace period of 30 days, or one month of not less than 30 days, for premiums after the first.

items.stem: James misses the annual premium on his $250,000 life policy, due March 1. He dies on March 20 without paying. The policy has a 30-day grace period. What does the beneficiary receive?
options: $250,000, less the unpaid premium
Nothing, because the premium was unpaid
$250,000, plus a refund of the last premium
Only the policy's cash surrender value
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-3 keeps the policy in full force during the grace period. If a claim arises then, the overdue premium (and any permitted interest) may be deducted from the amount payable.

items.stem: If a New Jersey life insurer charges interest when a premium is paid during the grace period, the rate may not exceed:
options: 4% per year
6% per year
8% per year
10% per year
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-3 lets the insurer charge interest for the days of grace used, at no more than 6% per year.

items.stem: A life policy has been in force for three years, and the insured is alive, when the insurer discovers he understated his weight on the application. Can the insurer now contest the policy's validity?
options: Yes, because any misstatement voids the policy
Yes, but only if the misstatement was material
Yes, within 30 days of discovering the misstatement
No, because the 2-year contestable period has passed
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-4 makes the policy incontestable, except for nonpayment of premiums, once it has been in force during the insured's lifetime for 2 years from issue.

items.stem: An insured dies 18 months after the policy was issued. The insurer then discovers a material misrepresentation on the application. Under New Jersey's incontestable provision, the insurer:
options: Can still contest, since 2 years did not pass in the insured's life
Has to pay, since death makes the policy incontestable
Has to pay, since contests end when the insured dies
Can contest after it first obtains a court order
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-4 makes a policy incontestable only after it has been in force during the insured's lifetime for 2 years. A death at 18 months means that period never ran, so the policy is still contestable.

items.stem: Under the entire contract provision, the contract between the insurer and the policyowner consists of:
options: The policy, plus the producer's sales materials
The policy, plus the application if a copy is attached
The policy, plus the insurer's bylaws
The application alone
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-5 makes the policy, with the application if a copy is attached or endorsed when issued, the entire contract. Outside documents such as bylaws or sales materials are not part of it.

items.stem: In the absence of fraud, statements an applicant makes on a New Jersey life insurance application are treated as:
options: Warranties
Conditions precedent
Guarantees
Representations
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-5 provides that, in the absence of fraud, statements in the application are deemed representations and not warranties.

items.stem: An insured stated her age as 45 on the application. She was actually 48. After her death, the insurer discovers the error. What happens?
options: The benefit is what the premium would buy at 48
The claim is denied for misrepresentation
The full face amount is paid as written
The premiums are refunded with interest
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-6 adjusts the amount payable to what the premium would have purchased at the correct age.

items.stem: A $100,000 life policy was issued based on a misstated age. At the insured's true age, the premium paid would have bought only $88,000 of coverage. At death, the insurer pays:
options: $100,000 minus the premium shortfall
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-6 pays the amount the premium would have purchased at the correct age, here $88,000.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, which dividend option must every participating ordinary life policy make available?
options: Paid-up additions
Cash
Reduction of premiums
Accumulation at interest
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-7 requires that any dividend be payable in cash at the owner's option, or applied to other options the policy may provide. Only the cash option is mandatory.

items.stem: A participating ordinary life policy in New Jersey must begin apportioning divisible surplus annually no later than the end of which policy year?
options: First
Second
Third
Fifth
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-7 requires annual apportionment beginning not later than the end of the third policy year. The fifth year applies only to industrial policies.

items.stem: A New Jersey ordinary whole life policy must offer a policy loan once it has a cash surrender value and how many full years' premiums have been paid?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-8 requires the insurer to advance a loan after 3 full years' premiums have been paid and the policy has a cash surrender value.

items.stem: Mia's whole life policy has built cash value after 2 full years of premiums, and she asks for a policy loan. Under New Jersey's policy loan provision, the insurer:
options: Is not yet required to offer a loan
Has to grant the loan on request
Has to lend up to half the cash value
Is not allowed to lend until year 5
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-8 requires a loan to be available only after 3 full years' premiums have been paid and the policy has a cash surrender value. After 2 years, the requirement has not been triggered.

items.stem: A New Jersey life insurer may delay granting a policy loan for up to 6 months, EXCEPT when the loan is:
options: Requested by an assignee of record
More than half the cash surrender value
Requested within the first policy year
Used to pay a premium to the insurer
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-8 lets the insurer defer a loan for 6 months, except a loan used to pay a premium to the insurer.

items.stem: A policyowner's loan balance plus interest grows until it exceeds the policy's loan value. Before the policy can terminate, the insurer must:
options: Mail at least 30 days' notice
Obtain the beneficiary's written consent
Convert it to reduced paid-up insurance
Wait until the next policy anniversary
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-8 allows termination when indebtedness equals or exceeds the loan value, but not until at least 30 days' notice has been mailed to the owner and any assignee of record.

items.stem: New Jersey's required policy loan provision does NOT apply to:
options: Ordinary whole life insurance
Term insurance
Limited-pay whole life insurance
Endowment insurance
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-8 states that the policy loan requirement does not apply to term insurance or industrial life policies.

items.stem: Unless it was surrendered for cash or its values are exhausted, a lapsed New Jersey ordinary life policy may be reinstated within what period after the first unpaid premium was due?
options: 6 months
1 year
2 years
3 years
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-9 allows reinstatement within 3 years (2 years for industrial policies) from the due date of the first premium in default.

items.stem: To reinstate a lapsed New Jersey life policy, which of the following is NOT a requirement?
options: Evidence of insurability satisfactory to the insurer
Payment of all premiums in arrears, with interest
Repayment or reinstatement of any policy loans
Approval of the reinstatement by the commissioner
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-9 requires a written application, satisfactory evidence of insurability, payment of premiums in arrears and repayment or reinstatement of any indebtedness, with interest. No commissioner approval is involved.

items.stem: A New Jersey life policy with a 2-year incontestable period is reinstated after a lapse. For how long can the insurer contest it because of misstatements in the reinstatement application?
options: For 2 years after reinstatement
Not at all after reinstatement
For whatever is left of the original 2 years
For as long as the policy stays in force
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-17 allows a reinstated policy to be contested for material misstatements in the reinstatement only for the same period, following reinstatement, as after original issue. New Jersey requires that period to be 2 years.

items.stem: For an uncontested death claim, a New Jersey life insurer must make settlement within how many days after receiving due proof of death?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-11 requires settlement within 60 days after receipt of due proof of death.

items.stem: A New Jersey life insurer receives due proof of death on May 1 and finds nothing that needs investigation. Settlement must be made no later than:
options: May 31
June 15
June 30
July 30
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-11 requires settlement within 60 days after receipt of due proof of death. 60 days after May 1 is June 30.

items.stem: If a New Jersey life insurer needs to investigate a death claim further, it must notify the claimant in writing, with the reason, no later than which day after receiving due proof of death?
options: 15th
30th
45th
60th
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-11 requires written notice, stating the reason, no later than the 45th calendar day when a claim needs more investigation or is denied.

items.stem: When a New Jersey life insurer pays a death claim late, the overdue payment:
options: Earns no interest unless the policy provides it
Earns interest at a rate tied to a State fund
Earns interest at a flat 18% per year
Earns interest only if a court orders it
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-11 makes overdue payments bear interest at the average rate of return of the State of New Jersey Cash Management Fund for the preceding fiscal year.

items.stem: After a premium default on a New Jersey ordinary life policy with cash value, the owner may choose a nonforfeiture option no later than how many days after the due date of the unpaid premium?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-19(a) requires the insurer to grant a paid-up nonforfeiture benefit, or another available option, on request no later than 60 days after the due date of the premium in default.

items.stem: A policyowner stops paying premiums on a whole life policy with cash value and never responds to the insurer's notices. The policy has no automatic premium loan provision. Under New Jersey's nonforfeiture law, what happens?
options: The policy lapses with no remaining value
The insurer mails the cash value to the owner
The insurer takes an automatic loan for future premiums
The paid-up benefit the policy specifies takes effect
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-19(a) requires that the paid-up nonforfeiture benefit specified in the policy take effect automatically unless the owner elects another option within 60 days.

items.stem: Under New Jersey's standard nonforfeiture law, an ordinary life policy must offer a cash surrender value on default once premiums have been paid for at least:
options: 1 full year
2 full years
3 full years
5 full years
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-19(a) requires a cash surrender value on surrender after a default once premiums have been paid for at least 3 full years on ordinary insurance (5 years for industrial).

items.stem: A participating policy offers several dividend options, and the owner never elects one. Under New Jersey law, the policy must:
options: Forfeit the dividend to the insurer's surplus
Hold the dividend until the owner files a written request
Name a default option for that case
Let the insurer pick a different option each year
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-7 requires a policy that offers other dividend options to state which option takes effect automatically if the owner does not elect another.

items.stem: A life policy delivered in New Jersey may not limit the time to bring a lawsuit on the policy to less than how long after the cause of action accrues?
options: 1 year
2 years
3 years
5 years
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-15 bars any life policy from limiting the time to commence an action to less than 5 years after the cause of action accrues.

items.stem: An insured dies without having elected a settlement option. The beneficiary would like the insurer to keep the proceeds and pay them out over time. Under New Jersey law:
options: The policyholder alone could have chosen that
The insurer and the beneficiary may agree to that
The insurer may do so after segregating the funds
The beneficiary has to take a lump sum
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-10 lets the insurer hold the proceeds at maturity under an agreement with the beneficiaries when the policyholder made no settlement agreement.

items.stem: An ordinary whole life policy has been continued as reduced paid-up insurance since its fifth anniversary. Its next anniversary is March 1. Under New Jersey's nonforfeiture law, what is the latest date after that anniversary on which the owner can surrender the policy and be owed its cash surrender value?
options: March 15
March 31
April 30
May 1
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-19(a) requires the insurer to pay a cash surrender value on a paid-up policy, including one continued under a paid-up nonforfeiture benefit that began on or after the third anniversary, when it is surrendered within 30 days after any policy anniversary. Thirty days after a March 1 anniversary is March 31.

items.stem: New Jersey lets an insurer substitute an alternative paid-up nonforfeiture benefit for the one stipulated in the policy if the alternative is actuarially equivalent and provides:
options: Less death benefit coverage, with a premium refund
More death benefit coverage, in amount or in duration
The same coverage, subject to new evidence of insurability
The same death benefit with a shorter premium-paying period
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-19(a) allows an actuarially equivalent alternative paid-up nonforfeiture benefit that provides a greater amount or longer period of death benefits.

items.stem: Under the extended term nonforfeiture option, what determines how long the term coverage lasts?
options: The face amount the owner chooses at lapse
The number of years premiums were paid, regardless of cash value
How much cash value there is and how old the insured is
The insurer's current dividend scale
items.explanation: Per NC DOI, Standard Policy Provisions and Optional Riders, extended term keeps the policy in force as term coverage to a future date, and its length depends on the policy's cash value and the insured's age.

items.stem: A whole life owner can no longer pay premiums but wants coverage that lasts for life with no further payments, even if the face amount is smaller. Which nonforfeiture option fits?
options: Extended term insurance
Cash surrender
Automatic premium loan
Reduced paid-up insurance
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, reduced paid-up insurance uses the cash value to buy a paid-up permanent policy with no further premiums, while extended term buys term coverage.

items.stem: A policyowner misses a premium and the grace period ends. The policy stays in force because the insurer paid the premium from the policy's own value, adding that amount to what the owner owes against the policy. Which provision did the owner elect?
options: Automatic premium loan
Waiver of premium
Extended term
Reinstatement
items.explanation: Per NC DOI, Standard Policy Provisions and Optional Riders, an automatic premium loan collects past-due premiums through a policy loan, which keeps the policy from lapsing if the loan value is enough. The owner usually must elect it.

items.stem: A beneficiary wants the insurer to hold the $200,000 death benefit and send her the earnings on it, leaving the principal intact for now. Which settlement option fits?
options: Fixed period
Interest only
Fixed amount
Life income
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, under the interest only option the insurance company keeps the benefits and pays the interest.

items.stem: A beneficiary wants the death benefit paid in equal installments over exactly 10 years, with the size of each payment set by that schedule. Which settlement option fits?
options: Fixed amount
Interest only
Fixed period
Life income
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, the fixed period option pays benefits over a predetermined number of months or years, while the fixed amount option pays a specified amount each period.

items.stem: A 70-year-old widow wants payments from her husband's death benefit that she cannot outlive. Which settlement option fits best?
options: Fixed period
Interest only
Lump sum
Life income
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, the life income option pays benefits for the life of the beneficiary.

items.stem: When a New Jersey insurer pays a premium automatically by a policy loan to prevent lapse, it must mail the policyholder a notice showing the loan amount and interest rate no later than:
options: 10 days after the premium due date
60 days after the premium due date
The next policy anniversary
30 days after the end of the grace period
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-10.1 requires written notice by regular mail, showing the loan amount and loan interest rate, no later than 30 days after the end of the grace period of the premium paid by loan.

items.stem: A New Jersey policyholder mails an overdue premium on the last day of the 30-day grace period, and the insurer receives it three days later. Under New Jersey rules, the payment is:
options: Late, since the insurer received it after the grace period
Late, so the policy lapses when the grace period ends
Timely, since payment counts as made on the date it was mailed
Timely only if sent by certified mail
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) makes payment effective on the date the policyholder mails it, bars requiring receipt within the grace period, and lets the insurer rely on the postmark.

items.stem: For a New Jersey universal life policy kept in force by its account value, one permitted grace period method is at least how long after the first monthly deduction date on which the value cannot cover a full month of insurance?
options: 30 days
31 days
60 days
90 days
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) allows a grace period for account value policies of no less than 30 days after the policy value reaches zero, or no less than 60 days after the first monthly deduction date for which the value is insufficient for a full month.

items.stem: Under New Jersey policy form rules, may an insurer cut off a policy's grace period early because the policy loans have grown too large?
options: Yes, once the loan exceeds the cash value
Yes, if it gives 10 days' written notice
No, unless the policy is term insurance
No, the grace period is in addition to the loan protections
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) bars a grace period provision that lets the grace period be preempted by termination for excessive loans. The grace period is in addition to the policy loan protections.

items.stem: An insured's true age turns out to be above the oldest issue age the insurer offers for that policy form. Under New Jersey rules, the insurer:
options: Extrapolates a premium and benefit for the true age
Rescinds the policy and refunds all premiums
Pays the full face amount, since the age error was not fraud
Converts the policy to term at the true age
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) requires the insurer to extrapolate a premium and benefit when the corrected age falls outside its issue ages, and bars a provision stating that the policy will be rescinded and premiums refunded.

items.stem: Under New Jersey policy form standards, a participating policy must allow the policyholder at least how long after a dividend becomes due to elect a dividend option?
options: 10 days
30 days
60 days
One policy year
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) requires the election period to be no less than 30 days following the date on which the dividend is due and payable.

items.stem: A New Jersey life policy charges a variable policy loan interest rate. How often must the insurer redetermine that rate, under New Jersey policy form standards?
options: At least every 24 months, and at most every 6 months
At least every 12 months, and at most every 3 months
At least every 6 months, and at most every month
At least every 5 years, and at most every year
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) requires a variable loan rate to be redetermined no less than once every 12 months but no more often than once every three months.

items.stem: A New Jersey policy has a variable loan interest rate, and the insurer plans to raise the rate. How much advance written notice must the policyholder get?
options: None, if the policy discloses the rate method
At least 30 days before the increase takes effect
At least 60 days before the next policy anniversary
At least 10 days before the increase takes effect
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b)7-9 requires the insurer to notify the policyholder in writing at least 10 days before the effective date of any increase in a variable loan rate.

items.stem: A New Jersey policyholder takes a cash loan from a policy with a variable loan interest rate. The insurer must notify her in writing of the initial loan rate no later than:
options: The next policy anniversary
10 days after the loan
30 days after the loan
90 days after the loan
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b)7-9 requires written notice of the initial rate at the time of a cash loan or as soon as practicable, but no later than 30 days following the loan.

items.stem: A policy's variable loan rate is reset every quarter. Midway through a policy year, a rate increase alone would push the loan balance past the loan value. Under New Jersey rules, the policy:
options: Cannot end that policy year merely because the rate went up
Terminates once the loan balance exceeds the loan value
Converts automatically to reduced paid-up insurance
Terminates after a 10-day notice
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b)7-9 requires a policy whose loan rate is redetermined more often than annually to state that it will not terminate in any policy year solely because of an interest rate change during that year.

items.stem: A universal life policy lapsed 14 months ago, and the owner now reinstates it. Under New Jersey rules, which charge may the insurer NOT require for reinstatement?
options: The monthly deduction for the grace period
Monthly deductions for the months of lapse after the grace period
Monthly deductions paid in advance for a stated number of future months
Evidence of insurability, if the provision states it
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b)7-9 lets the insurer require advance monthly deductions and the grace-period deduction, but bars charging monthly deductions for the period of default beyond the grace period. Reinstatement is offered for 3 years from default.

items.stem: Under New Jersey life policy form standards, once the insurer receives due proof of death and any other documents its policy requires, it must settle the death claim within:
options: 15 days
30 days
60 days
90 days
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b)10-13 requires the claims payment provision to state that settlement will be made within 60 days after receipt of the required proof and documents.

items.stem: Under New Jersey life policy form standards, the title on a policy's face page must state whether the policy is:
options: Participating or nonparticipating
Term or permanent
Fixed or variable
Individual or group
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b)10-13 requires the face-page title to briefly describe the policy, not mislead, and state whether the form is participating or nonparticipating.

items.stem: A beneficiary's death proceeds are placed in an insurer's retained asset account with a checkbook. Under New Jersey disclosure rules, the funds in this account are protected by:
options: The FDIC
The state life and health guaranty association
The Securities Investor Protection Corporation
The insurer's agent's errors and omissions coverage
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-61.3(a),(d) requires disclosure that retained asset account funds are not guaranteed by the FDIC but are guaranteed by the state guaranty associations.

items.stem: Under New Jersey's retained asset account rules, when must the insurer give a beneficiary information describing all available settlement options?
options: After the claim is paid
Only if the beneficiary asks in writing
At the policy's original delivery
Along with the claim paperwork
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-61.3(a),(d) requires the insurer to give all beneficiaries easy-to-understand information on all settlement options, provided with the claim form.

items.stem: A life policy excludes death while piloting a private aircraft. Five years after issue, the insured dies piloting his own plane. Under New Jersey law, the insurer may:
options: Not deny, since the policy is now incontestable
Deny only if the exclusion was in a separate rider
Not deny, since exclusions lapse after 2 years
Deny the claim under the aviation exclusion
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-16 provides that an incontestable clause bars only contests of the policy's validity. The insurer may still rely at any time on policy provisions that exclude or restrict coverage.

items.stem: When a New Jersey life policy is reinstated, the insurer may add an exclusion only if:
options: It was allowable at the policy's original issue
The policyowner agrees to pay a higher premium
The commissioner approves it in advance
It applies only to the first year after reinstatement
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-17 allows a reinstated policy to exclude or restrict liability to the same extent as could have been done at original issue, effective from the reinstatement date.

items.stem: An insured dies by suicide 14 months after a $300,000 policy was issued. The policy has a standard two-year suicide clause. The beneficiary will most likely receive:
options: A sum equal to what the owner paid in
The full $300,000 death benefit
Nothing at all
Half of the death benefit
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations and NC DOI, Standard Policy Provisions and Optional Riders, a suicide clause lets the insurer refuse the death claim for a suicide within the first two years, but the insurer must return the premiums paid.

items.stem: An insured dies by suicide three years after his policy was issued. The policy has a standard two-year suicide clause and has stayed in force. The insurer will:
options: Return the premiums paid instead of the face amount
Pay the full death benefit
Deny the claim, since suicide is a permanent exclusion
Pay the face amount less three years of premiums
items.explanation: Per NC DOI, Standard Policy Provisions and Optional Riders, the suicide clause limits the benefit to premiums paid only for a suicide within the first two years. After that period, the full death benefit is payable.

items.stem: A New Jersey policy shows a policy date of March 1 and an issue date of March 20, with no backdating to save age. When do the incontestable and suicide periods begin?
options: March 20, the issue date
The date the policy is delivered
March 1, the earlier of the two dates
The date the first premium is paid
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) starts the incontestability and suicide periods on the earliest of the date of issue, the policy date and any other effective date, except when backdating saves age.

items.stem: Five years after issue, a policyowner raises his face amount from $250,000 to $400,000 after a new medical exam. The policy form reserves the insurer's right to contest such increases. Under New Jersey rules, what may the insurer contest?
options: The full $400,000 for two years from the increase
Nothing, since the original policy is past its contestable period
The $250,000 original amount, for one more year
The $150,000 increase, for up to two years from the increase
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) lets the insurer reserve a right to contest for no more than two additional years after an increase bought with new evidence of insurability, limited to the actual increase.

items.stem: A policy's cost-of-living rider automatically raises the face amount, with no new application or medical evidence. Under New Jersey rules, the increase:
options: Is not contestable at all
Starts a new two-year contestable period on the increase
Is contestable for one year from the increase
Is contestable until the next policy anniversary
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) bars insurers from retaining any right to contest modifications made without additional evidence of insurability, such as corridor or cost-of-living increases.

items.stem: A term policy issued 18 months ago is converted, at the same face amount and with no increase in the amount at risk, to whole life. The insured dies by suicide 8 months after the conversion. Under New Jersey rules:
options: The suicide exclusion applies, since the whole life policy is only 8 months old
The suicide exclusion does not apply, since the period began with the original policy
The insurer returns premiums paid on the whole life policy only
The claim is contestable for misstatements in the conversion
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.3(b) starts the suicide period under the new policy on the original policy's issue date when a conversion does not increase the amount at risk. Here 26 months have passed, so the two-year period has ended.

items.stem: A policy has a New Jersey-compliant military war exclusion. The insured is wounded in combat while serving, leaves the service, and dies of those wounds eight months later. Can the insurer apply the exclusion?
options: Yes, since the cause of death occurred in service
Yes, for any death from a war wound at any time
No, since war exclusions apply only to civilians
No, since death occurred more than six months after service ended
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.4 lets a military war exclusion apply only if death occurs while in the forces or within six months after service ends. Eight months after discharge is outside that window.

items.stem: Under New Jersey rules, a civilian war exclusion may apply to a death from war outside the home area only within how long after the policy's issue date?
options: Six months
One year
Two years
Five years
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.4 allows a civilian war exclusion for death from war outside the home area only within two years from the date of issue, while the insured is not in military forces or units.

items.stem: An insured dies in an aviation accident that the policy excludes. Premiums paid total $9,000, and the policy reserve is $12,500, with no loans, dividends or withdrawals. Under New Jersey rules, the insurer must pay at least:
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.4 requires that any amount payable for a death from an excluded act be at least the greater of premiums paid or the reserve, adjusted for dividends, loans, withdrawals and surrenders. The greater of $9,000 and $12,500 is $12,500.

items.stem: How must the policyowner be notified when a New Jersey life policy includes a war risk exclusion?
options: By a stamp across the face of the policy
By a separate letter mailed after delivery
By a footnote in the illustration
By a verbal disclosure from the producer
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.4 requires the policyowner to be notified of war, aviation or avocation exclusions, and requires war risk exclusion notice in the form of a stamp across the face of the policy.

items.stem: Under New Jersey life policy form rules, a pre-existing condition exclusion may apply to which part of a life policy?
options: The base death benefit
Disability benefits
The cash surrender value
The accidental death benefit
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.7(a)1-2 permits pre-existing condition exclusions only for disability benefits.

items.stem: An applicant discloses a back condition on her life application. The insurer issues the policy with a disability waiver of premium benefit and attaches no exclusion rider. Six months later she is disabled by that back condition. The insurer:
options: May deny the claim during the first two years
May deny the claim as pre-existing
Is liable after a 12-month waiting period
Must pay, starting from when coverage began
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.7(a)1-2 makes the insurer liable from the policy's effective date for disability from a pre-existing condition that was in the application and not excluded by rider.

items.stem: While processing a life application, a producer notices the applicant left the tobacco-use question blank and wants to fill it in. Under New Jersey law, the producer:
options: Must get the insurer's written approval first
Must get the applicant's written consent first
Must get the beneficiary's written consent first
Must initial the change and then tell the applicant
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-3 bars anyone other than the applicant from altering a written application without the applicant's written consent.

items.stem: Which change to a written life application may be made without the applicant's written consent?
options: Producer corrections of spelling errors in answers
Insurer updates to the applicant's medical history
Producer additions of omitted answers from notes
Insurer office codes visibly not the applicant's
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-3 allows only insurer insertions for administrative purposes, made so they clearly are not attributed to the applicant. Other alterations need the applicant's written consent.

items.stem: An applicant overstated his height by one inch. Under the insurer's guidelines, his correct height would have produced the same underwriting decision and premium. He dies within the contestable period. Under New Jersey law, the insurer:
options: May deny, since the policy is still contestable
Must pay, since the misstatement was not material
May reduce the benefit to reflect the correct height
May deny the claim but must refund the premiums
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-3 provides that a false statement in the application does not bar recovery unless it materially affected the acceptance of the risk or the hazard assumed. Being within the contestable period does not change that.

items.stem: In a lawsuit over a New Jersey life policy, the insurer wants to rely on statements in the application. The application is admissible only if:
options: It was made part of the policy at issue
The applicant signed it in the producer's presence
The insurer kept the original for at least five years
The application form was filed with the commissioner
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-3 makes an application inadmissible in any action on the policy unless a copy was attached to or endorsed on the policy when issued.

items.stem: After a New Jersey life policy is reinstated, the insured asks in writing for a copy of the reinstatement application. The insurer must deliver or mail it within:
options: 10 days
15 days
30 days
60 days
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-3 requires the insurer to deliver or mail a copy of the reinstatement or renewal application within 30 days after receiving a written request at its home office.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, a minor may contract for life insurance on his own life beginning at age:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-2 allows any minor not less than 15 years of age to contract for insurance or annuities on his own life, or on another person in whom he has an insurable interest.

items.stem: A 16-year-old beneficiary with no appointed guardian may give the insurer a valid receipt for payments totaling up to what amount in a calendar year?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-2 deems a minor 15 or older competent to receive and acknowledge insurance payments of up to $2,000 in any calendar year, if the insurer has no notice of a guardian.

items.stem: A client has decided to replace an existing life policy with a new one. When should the old policy be canceled?
options: Once the new application is signed
Once the first new premium is paid
Once the insurer orders a medical exam
Once the new policy has been received
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, if you decide to replace a policy, do not cancel the old one until you have received the new one.

items.stem: One reason replacing a life policy can be costly is that:
options: The up-front costs of a new contract may be paid all over again
The old policy's death benefit is reduced once a new application is filed
The new policy's premiums are based on the age at which the old one was issued
The new policy cannot name the same beneficiary as the old one
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide, much of what was paid in the early years of a policy covered the company's cost of selling and issuing it, and a new policy may charge that cost again.

items.stem: A producer takes a life application, and the applicant states in the signed existing-coverage statement that she owns no other life policies or annuities. Under New Jersey's replacement rules, the producer:
options: Still has to read the replacement notice aloud
Has to notify every insurer the applicant has used
Has to leave a policy summary of the new policy
Has completed her replacement duties
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.3 requires a statement signed by the applicant and producer on existing coverage. If the answer is no, the producer's duties with respect to replacement are complete.

items.stem: In a New Jersey replacement, when must the producer present the replacement notice to the applicant and offer to read it?
options: Before the policy is delivered
Within 5 business days after the application
At the start of the free look period
No later than when the application is taken
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.3 requires the producer to present and offer to read the replacement notice not later than at the time of taking the application.

items.stem: Who must sign the New Jersey replacement notice?
options: Both the applicant and the producer
The applicant alone
The producer alone
The applicant and the existing insurer
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.3 requires the replacement notice to be signed by both the applicant and the producer, and it remains with the applicant.

items.stem: A producer used a printed brochure and a printed, personalized illustration while replacing a client's old policy. Under New Jersey rules, when must the client receive the original or a copy of this sales material?
options: When the new policy is delivered
When the application is completed
Within 5 business days after the sale
Only if the client asks for them
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.3 requires the producer, in a replacement, to give the applicant the original or a copy of all sales material at the time the application is completed. Electronic material must be printed no later than delivery.

items.stem: After receiving a completed application that involves replacement, a New Jersey replacing insurer must notify the existing insurer within:
options: 3 business days
5 business days
10 calendar days
30 calendar days
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.4 requires the replacing insurer to notify any affected existing insurer within five business days of receiving a completed application indicating replacement.

items.stem: When a new life policy replaces an existing one in New Jersey, the owner may return the new policy for a full refund within how many days of delivery?
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.4 requires the replacing insurer to give notice of the right to return the policy within 30 days of delivery for an unconditional full refund. A non-replacement policy has a 10-day minimum.

items.stem: A policyowner replaces an 18-month-old policy with a new one from the same insurer, for the same face amount. How do the new policy's contestable and suicide periods work under New Jersey rules?
options: Both start over from the new issue date
They are waived because the insurer is the same
Time already served under the old policy counts toward both
The suicide period restarts, but the contestable period is credited
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.4 requires a replacing insurer that is the same as or affiliated with the existing insurer to credit the time elapsed under the replaced policy's incontestability and suicide periods, up to the old face amount.

items.stem: An insurer receives notice that one of its policies is about to be replaced by another company's policy. Under New Jersey rules, what is this existing insurer required to do?
options: Within five business days, send the replacing insurer the old policy's illustration
Within five business days, tell the owner in writing to keep paying premiums on the old policy
Within thirty days, tell the owner in writing about the 30-day right to return the new policy
Within five business days, tell the owner in writing about a right to see current policy values
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-2.6 requires the existing insurer to notify the owner in writing, within five business days of receiving the replacement notice, of the right to receive information on the existing policy's values, such as an in force illustration.

items.stem: An insurer orders an investigative consumer report on a life insurance applicant. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, written disclosure must be mailed or delivered to the applicant no later than how many days after the report is first requested?
options: 3 days
5 days
10 days
30 days
items.explanation: 15 U.S.C. § 1681d(a)-(b) requires written disclosure of an investigative consumer report to be mailed or delivered no later than three days after the report was first requested.

items.stem: After learning of an investigative consumer report, an applicant asks in writing about the nature and scope of the investigation. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the insurer must respond in writing within:
options: 3 days
5 days
10 days
30 days
items.explanation: 15 U.S.C. § 1681d(a)-(b) requires a complete written disclosure of the nature and scope of the investigation within five days after the consumer's request is received or the report was first requested, whichever is later.

items.stem: To underwrite a large life policy, an insurer hires a firm to interview an applicant's neighbors and coworkers about his lifestyle and reputation. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, this is:
options: A Medical Information Bureau report
A motor vehicle record
An attending physician statement
An investigative consumer report
items.explanation: 15 U.S.C. § 1681d(a)-(b) describes an investigative consumer report as one including information on the person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics and mode of living, and it requires written disclosure to the person.

items.stem: An insurer declines a life insurance application based partly on information in a consumer report. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the insurer must:
options: Notify the applicant of the adverse action
Refund the application fee within 30 days
Re-underwrite the application after six months
Report the declination to the commissioner
items.explanation: 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a) requires anyone taking adverse action based in whole or part on a consumer report to give the consumer notice of the adverse action, along with other disclosures.

items.stem: An adverse action notice based on a consumer report must include a statement that the consumer reporting agency:
options: Did not make the decision and cannot give the reasons
Reviewed and approved the insurer's decision
Will reconsider the decision on written request
Shares legal responsibility for the decision
items.explanation: 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a) requires a statement that the consumer reporting agency did not make the decision and is unable to provide the specific reasons for it.

items.stem: After an adverse action based on a consumer report, the notice must tell the applicant of the right to a free copy of the report, requested within how many days?
items.explanation: 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a) requires notice of the right to a free copy of the consumer report, including an indication of the 60-day period for obtaining it.

items.stem: An adverse action notice must tell the applicant of the right to dispute the accuracy of the consumer report with:
options: The insurer's underwriting department
The consumer reporting agency
The state insurance commissioner
The producer who took the application
items.explanation: 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a) requires notice of the consumer's right to dispute the accuracy or completeness of the report with the consumer reporting agency that furnished it.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, which of these may NOT be used as a basis for charging a higher life insurance premium?
options: The applicant's ancestry
The applicant's medical history
The applicant's hazardous hobbies
The applicant's tobacco use
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-12(a)-(c) bars discrimination because of race, creed, color, national origin or ancestry in issuing life insurance or fixing its rates, terms or conditions.

items.stem: Two applicants are the same age and sex, in the same health, and in the same underwriting class. The insurer charges one of them a higher rate because of the agent who submitted the application. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Permitted, since agents may negotiate rates
Not permitted, because every applicant must pay an identical rate
Permitted, if the higher rate is disclosed at delivery
Not permitted, because it unfairly discriminates within one class
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-12(a)-(c) bars unfair discrimination between individuals of the same class and equal expectation of life in the rates charged for life insurance.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, a new individual life policy that is not a replacement must give the policyholder a free look period of at least how many days to cancel for a refund?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-2.1 requires a period of no less than 10 days after the policyholder receives the policy to cancel and receive a prompt refund.

items.stem: A New Jersey life policy is issued on May 1, and the agent delivers it to the policyholder on May 8. The minimum free look period ends no earlier than:
options: May 11
May 15
May 18
May 31
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-2.1 starts the free look period on the date the policyholder receives the policy. Ten days after May 8 is May 18.

items.stem: A policyholder returns her new life policy with a written cancellation request on day 6 of the free look period. She paid a $1,200 premium plus a $50 policy fee. Her refund is:
options: $0, since the policy was already issued
$1,200, since fees are not refundable
$1,250, the premium plus the policy fee
$1,200 less a pro-rata charge for 6 days of coverage
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-2.1 requires a prompt refund of any premium paid, including any policy fees or other charges, when the policy is cancelled during the free look period.

items.stem: How does a New Jersey policyholder exercise the free look right on a new life policy?
options: By sending it back to the company with a signed note to cancel
By calling the agent and asking to cancel within the period
By simply not paying the second premium when it comes due
By filing a complaint with the Department of Banking and Insurance
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-2.1 requires mailing or otherwise surrendering the policy to the insurer together with a written request for cancellation.

items.stem: New Jersey's 10-day free look requirement for life policies does NOT apply to:
options: Industrial life insurance
Group life insurance
Variable life insurance
Juvenile life insurance
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-2.1 applies to policies of life insurance other than group insurance.

items.stem: A New Jersey life policy includes an unconditional 10-day refund provision. What is the latest point at which the insurer may provide the Buyer's Guide?
options: Before the initial premium is accepted
Before the application is taken
With the policy at delivery
After the free look period ends
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-11.3 requires the Buyer's Guide before accepting the initial premium, but if the policy has an unconditional refund provision of at least 10 days, the guide may be delivered with the policy or before delivery.

items.stem: A New Jersey life policy has no unconditional refund provision. The producer collects the first premium with the application. Under New Jersey disclosure rules, the Buyer's Guide must be provided:
options: With the policy at delivery
Within 30 days after the policy is issued
On request only
Before the initial premium is accepted
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-11.3 requires the Buyer's Guide to be provided before the insurer accepts the applicant's initial premium, unless the policy has an unconditional refund provision of at least 10 days.

items.stem: A New Jersey policyowner asks the insurer for a statement of policy data on her existing policy. The insurer may charge a fee of no more than:
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-11.3 lets the insurer charge a reasonable fee, not to exceed $10.00, to prepare the statement of policy data, which covers 20 years from the previous anniversary unless otherwise requested.

items.stem: Under the federal telemarketing rules that apply to insurance sales calls, a producer may make a telephone solicitation to a residence only between:
options: 7 a.m. and 10 p.m., the caller's local time
8 a.m. and 9 p.m., the caller's local time
8 a.m. and 9 p.m., the called party's local time
9 a.m. and 8 p.m., the called party's local time
items.explanation: 47 C.F.R. § 64.1200(c) bars telephone solicitations to a residential subscriber before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m., local time at the called party's location.

items.stem: A New Jersey producer wants to make a sales call at 6:30 p.m. Eastern time to a prospect at home in California, where it is 3:30 p.m. Under the federal calling-hour rule, the call is:
options: Prohibited, because it is after 6 p.m. for the caller
Prohibited, because interstate sales calls need written consent
Permitted only with a recorded disclosure at the start
Permitted, because it is 3:30 p.m. where the prospect is
items.explanation: 47 C.F.R. § 64.1200(c) measures the 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. window by local time at the called party's location. 3:30 p.m. in California is within it.

items.stem: A producer wants to call a prospect whose number is on the national do-not-call registry. Which of the following allows the sales call?
options: The prospect's number is already in the agency's database
The prospect's neighbor referred the agency 2 months ago
The prospect visited the agency's website 6 months ago
The prospect bought a policy from the agency 10 months ago
items.explanation: 47 C.F.R. § 64.1200(f)(15) excludes from telephone solicitation a call to a person with whom the caller has an established business relationship, such as a purchase within the past 18 months.

items.stem: Under the federal do-not-call rules, an established business relationship based on a client's purchase lasts for how long after the purchase?
options: 3 months
6 months
12 months
18 months
items.explanation: 47 C.F.R. § 64.1200(f) bases an established business relationship on a purchase or transaction within the 18 months before the call.

items.stem: A client bought a single-premium policy from an agency, then surrendered it 20 months ago and has had no dealings with the agency since. Her number is on the national do-not-call registry. May the agency make a sales call to her?
options: No, because the business relationship exemption has expired
Yes, because she is a former customer
Yes, because registrations expire after five years
Yes, as long as the call is made before 9 p.m.
items.explanation: 47 C.F.R. § 64.1200(f) bases an established business relationship on a purchase or transaction within the 18 months before the call. At 20 months with no further dealings, it has ended, so the registry applies.
