items.stem: A prospect asked an agency about a life policy but did not buy. Under the federal do-not-call rules, the established business relationship from that inquiry lasts:
options: 30 days
3 months
6 months
18 months
items.explanation: 47 C.F.R. § 64.1200(f) bases an established business relationship on an inquiry or application within the three months before the call.

items.stem: A consumer put her number on the national do-not-call registry six years ago and has done nothing since. What is the status of her registration?
options: It expired after five years
It must be renewed before it is honored
It covers only calls from in-state sellers
It is still in effect
items.explanation: 47 C.F.R. § 64.1200(c) requires national registrations to be honored indefinitely, until the consumer cancels them or the administrator removes the number.

items.stem: A client who bought a policy from an agency last year tells the producer on a call, "Please don't call me with sales offers anymore." Her number is not on the national registry. What must the agency do?
options: Keep calling until her number appears on the national registry
Log the request and put her number on its internal list
Stop only the producer she spoke with from calling
Wait for her written confirmation before changing anything
items.explanation: 47 C.F.R. § 64.1200(d)(3) requires a caller that receives a do-not-call request to record it and place the number on its do-not-call list at the time the request is made.

items.stem: A policyowner assigns her life policy to a bank as collateral for a loan. Until the insurer receives written notice at its home office that the assignment has ended, the insurer:
options: May deal with the policyowner and disregard the assignment
Has to wait for a court to approve the assignment
Has to suspend the beneficiary designation
May deal with the bank under the terms of the assignment
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-4 entitles the insurer to deal with the assignee as owner or pledgee under the assignment's terms until it receives written notice of termination at its home office.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, how may a life policyowner assign the policy, subject to the policy's own terms on assignability?
options: By pledge or by transfer of title
With the beneficiary's written consent
By transfer of title, but not by pledge
To the issuing insurer, but not to a lender
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-4 allows such a policy to be assigned by pledge or by transfer of title through an assignment executed by the insured or owner alone and delivered to the insurer, whether or not the assignee is the insurer.

items.stem: A divorced woman is required by her divorce decree to pay alimony to her former husband. May she buy a life policy on him under New Jersey law?
options: No, since only the person receiving alimony may insure the payer
Yes, because of that obligation
No, since the marriage has ended
Yes, but with a court's approval
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-1.1 allows an individual liable for the support of a child or former spouse to procure insurance on that child or former spouse.

items.stem: A stranger with no insurable interest buys a policy on a man's life, names himself beneficiary and collects the death benefit. Under New Jersey law, who may sue the stranger to recover the benefits?
options: The insurer, which may sue to recover the payment
The Department of Banking and Insurance
The insured's employer
The insured's estate, through its personal representative
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-1.1 lets the individual insured, or his executor or administrator, sue to recover benefits paid to a payee under a contract made without the required insurable interest.

items.stem: An applicant falsely tells the insurer he is the insured's business partner. The insurer, with no reason to doubt him, issues the policy. Later the insured's family claims the insurer should have caught the lie. Under New Jersey law, the insurer:
options: Is not liable, since it may rely on the applicant's statements
Is liable, since it must independently verify insurable interest
Has to refund all premiums to the insured's estate
Is liable, unless the policy is past its contestable period
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-1.1 entitles the insurer to rely on the applicant's statements about insurable interest and bars legal liability, except as the policy provides, for untrue statements it relied on in good faith.

items.stem: New Jersey's statutory insurable interest requirements for life insurance do NOT apply to:
options: Individual annuities
Group life insurance
Industrial life insurance
Juvenile life insurance
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:24-1.1 states that it does not apply to group life insurance, group health insurance, blanket insurance or group annuities.

items.stem: An employer provides group term life insurance to employees. The cost of coverage above what amount is generally included in the employee's taxable income?
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 79 includes in an employee's income the cost of employer-provided group-term life insurance only to the extent it exceeds the cost of $50,000 of coverage, less any amount the employee paid.

items.stem: An employee has $150,000 of employer group term life coverage. The table cost of the excess coverage is $240 for the year, and the employee paid $60 toward the coverage through payroll deduction. How much is included in his taxable income?
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 79 taxes the cost of coverage above $50,000 only to the extent it exceeds what the employee paid. $240 minus $60 is $180.

items.stem: For federal tax purposes, the taxable cost of an employee's group term life coverage over $50,000 is measured by:
options: The employer's actual premium for that employee
IRS uniform premium rates set by 5-year age brackets
The employee's individual underwriting class
The policy's cash surrender value
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 79 measures the cost of group-term insurance using uniform premiums computed on 5-year age brackets prescribed by IRS regulations.

items.stem: An employee has $200,000 of employer group term life coverage and names a qualified charity as sole beneficiary for the entire tax year. How much of the cost of the excess coverage is taxable to the employee?
options: None of it
The cost above $50,000
The full cost of $200,000 of coverage
Half the cost above $50,000
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 79 excepts from income the cost of group-term coverage for which a qualified charity is the sole beneficiary for the entire period of the tax year.

items.stem: An early distribution from a qualified retirement plan, with no exception available, is generally hit with an additional tax equal to what percentage of the taxable amount?
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 72(t)(1)-(2)(A) adds a tax of 10 percent of the portion of an early distribution that is includible in gross income.

items.stem: An employee who is still working for her employer takes a distribution from the company's qualified plan. She avoids the 10% early distribution tax, without relying on any other exception, once she reaches age:
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 72(t)(1)-(2)(A) exempts distributions made on or after age 59½. The age-55 exception applies only after separation from service, so it does not help an employee who is still working.

items.stem: An employee leaves his job at age 56 and takes a distribution from that employer's qualified plan. The 10% early distribution tax:
options: Does not apply, since he left the job after turning 55
Applies, since he is under 59½
Applies, since the plan is a qualified plan
Does not apply, since any job change waives it
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 72(t)(1)-(2)(A) exempts distributions made to an employee after separation from service after reaching age 55.

items.stem: A client opens and funds her first Roth IRA at age 58 and withdraws earnings two years later at age 60. Is the withdrawal a qualified distribution?
options: Yes, because she is over age 59½
Yes, because Roth IRA earnings are tax-free at any age
No, because qualified distributions begin at age 62
No, because the 5-year period has not yet run
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 408A(d)(1)-(2) excludes a distribution made within the 5-taxable-year period that begins with the first year of a Roth IRA contribution, even if the owner is over 59½.

items.stem: A retiree born in 1956 turns 72 in 2028. Under current federal law, his applicable age for required minimum distributions is:
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(9)(C)(v) sets the applicable age at 73 for anyone who reaches 72 after December 31, 2022, and 73 before January 1, 2033. Age 75 applies to those who reach 74 after 2032.

items.stem: A company owned a policy on a staff accountant who was not a director or highly compensated when the policy was issued. Notice and consent were properly obtained. He left the company and died 5 years later. How are the death proceeds the company receives treated for income tax?
options: Taxable to the extent they exceed the premiums the company paid
Fully excluded, since notice and consent were obtained
Fully taxable, with no credit for premiums paid
Excluded, since key person coverage is tax-free
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(j) limits the exclusion to the premiums and other amounts paid unless an exception applies. Notice and consent alone are not enough; the insured must also fit an exception, such as being an employee within 12 months before death.

items.stem: A company with proper notice and consent owns a policy on a sales manager, who dies while still employed there. The death proceeds the company receives are:
options: Taxable above the premiums paid, since the company owns the policy
Taxable, since the company was the beneficiary
Excluded, but reduced by the cash value at death
Fully excluded from the company's gross income
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(j) keeps the full exclusion, when notice and consent were met, for an insured who was an employee at any time during the 12 months before death.

items.stem: For employer-owned life insurance, when must the employee receive written notice and give written consent?
options: Before the policy is issued
Within 30 days after the policy is issued
Before the employer files a death claim
Within 12 months after employment ends
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(j) requires the employee's written notice and consent before the issuance of the contract.

items.stem: Under federal tax rules on employer-owned life insurance, the employer's written notice to the employee must state:
options: The premium the employer will pay each year
The employee's own share of the cash value
The rating class the insurer assigned
The maximum face amount for which the employee could be insured
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(j) requires written notice of the employer's intent to insure the employee and of the maximum face amount for which the employee could be insured.

items.stem: Under the Social Security Act, a worker becomes fully insured, whatever his or her age, once he or she has earned how many quarters of coverage?
items.explanation: 42 U.S.C. § 414(a)-(b) treats anyone with 40 quarters of coverage as fully insured.

items.stem: A worker dies young with only a short work history. To be currently insured under Social Security, she needed at least:
options: 4 quarters of coverage in the last 8 quarters
6 quarters of coverage in the 13-quarter period ending with her death
20 quarters of coverage in the last 40 quarters
40 quarters of coverage in total
items.explanation: 42 U.S.C. § 414(a)-(b) defines a currently insured individual as one with at least six quarters of coverage in the thirteen-quarter period ending with the quarter of death or entitlement.

items.stem: A worker born in 1966 reaches age 62 in 2028. Her Social Security full retirement age is:
options: 66 and 6 months
items.explanation: 42 U.S.C. § 416(l)(1)-(2) sets retirement age at 67 for anyone who reaches early retirement age after December 31, 2021.

items.stem: What is the earliest age at which a worker can start reduced Social Security retirement benefits on his own work record?
items.explanation: 42 U.S.C. § 416(l)(1)-(2) sets early retirement age at 62 for an old-age benefit. Age 60 applies to a widow's or widower's benefit, not a worker's own retirement benefit.

items.stem: Maria's beneficiary receives a $300,000 lump-sum death benefit from her life policy. For federal income tax purposes, the death benefit is generally:
options: Fully taxable as ordinary income
Taxable only above the premiums Maria paid
Taxed as a long-term capital gain
Excluded from the beneficiary's gross income
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(a)(1) excludes from gross income amounts received under a life insurance contract that are paid by reason of the insured's death, whether in a lump sum or otherwise.

items.stem: An unrelated investor buys an existing $500,000 life policy from the insured for $60,000, then pays $40,000 in premiums before the insured dies. Under the transfer-for-value rule, how much of the death benefit is excluded from the investor's income?
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(a)(2) limits the exclusion after a transfer for value to the consideration paid plus premiums the transferee paid later: $60,000 + $40,000 = $100,000. The other $400,000 is taxable.

items.stem: Under Section 1035, which of the following exchanges can be made without recognizing gain or loss?
options: A life insurance policy for an annuity
An annuity for a life insurance policy
An annuity for a bank certificate of deposit
A life insurance policy for mutual fund shares
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 1035(a) allows a life insurance contract to be exchanged tax-free for another life contract, an endowment, an annuity or a qualified long-term care contract. An annuity cannot be exchanged tax-free for life insurance.

items.stem: A client wants to exchange her deferred annuity under Section 1035 without recognizing gain. Which of the following can she receive in the exchange?
options: A whole life policy
A term life policy
Another annuity contract
An endowment policy
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 1035(a)(3) allows an annuity to be exchanged tax-free only for another annuity or a qualified long-term care insurance contract, not for life or endowment insurance.

items.stem: Which of the following exchanges would NOT qualify for tax-free treatment under Section 1035?
options: An annuity for a life policy
A life policy for another life policy
A life policy for an annuity
An annuity for another annuity
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 1035(a)(3) allows an annuity to be exchanged tax-free only for another annuity or a qualified long-term care contract. Exchanging an annuity for life insurance does not qualify.

items.stem: A 52-year-old withdraws $20,000 from a nonqualified deferred annuity. $8,000 of it is taxable earnings, and no exception applies. What is the additional federal penalty tax?
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 72(q) adds a tax of 10 percent of the portion of the distribution includible in gross income: 10% of the $8,000 taxable portion is $800.

items.stem: The 10% federal penalty on premature annuity distributions does not apply to distributions made on or after the date the taxpayer reaches age:
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 72(q)(2)(A) exempts from the 10% penalty any distribution made on or after the date the taxpayer reaches age 59½.

items.stem: A 61-year-old withdraws $10,000 of taxable earnings from a nonqualified deferred annuity. The additional 10% federal penalty tax on this withdrawal is:
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 72(q)(2)(A) exempts from the 10% penalty any distribution made on or after the taxpayer reaches age 59½. At 61, no penalty applies.

items.stem: A life insurance policy issued in 2026 is classified as a modified endowment contract when it:
options: Does not pass the 7-pay test
Builds cash value above the premiums paid
Meets the 7-pay test but carries a large loan
Has a face amount over $1 million
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 7702A(a) defines a modified endowment contract as a life contract entered into on or after June 21, 1988 that fails the 7-pay test.

items.stem: A policyowner exchanges a modified endowment contract for a new life insurance policy. For tax purposes, the new policy is:
options: Also a modified endowment contract
A standard life policy if it passes the 7-pay test
A standard life policy once 7 years pass
A modified endowment contract only if surrendered
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 7702A(a)(2) treats any contract received in exchange for a modified endowment contract as a modified endowment contract itself.

items.stem: Carla pays $3,000 a year in premiums on a life policy on her own life, with her husband as beneficiary. On her federal income tax return, the premiums are:
options: Fully deductible
Deductible only above 7.5% of income
Deductible as a charitable gift
Not deductible
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 264(a)(1) allows no deduction for life insurance premiums when the taxpayer is directly or indirectly a beneficiary, which is the case for a personally owned policy benefiting her family.

items.stem: A nonqualified deferred annuity (not an IRA or employer plan) pays out before the holder reaches age 59½. Which of the following distributions is exempt from the 10% federal penalty?
options: A withdrawal to pay college tuition
A payment to the beneficiary after the holder's death
A withdrawal to buy a first home
A withdrawal made during the surrender charge period
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 72(q)(2)(B)-(C) exempts nonqualified annuity distributions made on or after the holder's death, or attributable to disability, from the 10% penalty. The tuition and first-home exceptions belong to the qualified-plan and IRA rules, not to nonqualified annuities.

items.stem: An insured who is terminally ill receives an accelerated death benefit from her life policy. Under federal tax law, the payment is treated as:
options: Ordinary income in the year received
An amount paid by reason of the insured's death
A taxable return of the premiums paid
A policy loan that must be repaid
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(g)(1) treats amounts received under a life insurance contract on the life of a terminally ill insured as paid by reason of death, so they qualify for the death benefit exclusion.

items.stem: Federal tax law treats accelerated death benefits favorably when the insured is terminally ill, or when the insured is:
options: Chronically ill
Seriously ill
Critically ill, as the insurer defines it
Mentally ill
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 101(g)(1) covers amounts received on the life of an insured who is terminally ill or chronically ill.

items.stem: In a viatical settlement, who pays the future premiums and collects the death benefit?
options: The original owner, who keeps the policy
The insurer that issued the policy
The third party that bought the policy
The insured's named beneficiary
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, the viatical settlement provider becomes the new owner, pays future premiums and collects the death benefit when the insured dies.

items.stem: New Jersey rules let an insurer define the terminal-illness trigger for accelerated death benefits as a life expectancy of anywhere from:
options: 3 to 12 months or less
6 to 24 months or less
12 to 36 months or less
24 to 60 months or less
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-30.3 requires the definition of a drastically limited life span to have a minimum of six months or less and a maximum of 24 months or less, as specified in the policy.

items.stem: A $200,000 policy pays $50,000 as an accelerated death benefit while the insured is terminally ill. Assuming no loans or other charges, what happens to the death benefit?
options: It stays at $200,000 until the insured dies
It drops to the policy's cash value
It is reduced by twice the amount paid
It is reduced by the amount paid early
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-30.3 defines accelerated death benefits as an advance payment of death proceeds to the owner during the insured's lifetime that reduces the death benefit otherwise payable.

items.stem: New Jersey permits accelerated death benefit provisions in which two forms?
options: A surrender of the policy or a lien on the death benefits
A policy loan or a dividend advance
A viatical sale or a reinstatement
An annuity conversion or a paid-up addition
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-30.4 permits accelerated death benefit provisions in the form of either a surrender of the policy or a lien on the death benefits.

items.stem: A policy with a $100,000 death benefit and $30,000 of cash value accelerates 40% of the death benefit under the surrender approach. What is the remaining cash value?
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-30.5 reduces the cash value by the same percentage as the death benefit under the surrender approach. Cutting $30,000 by 40% leaves $18,000.

items.stem: A $200,000 policy has a $40,000 outstanding loan. The owner accelerates $50,000 (25%) of the death benefit under the surrender approach. Under New Jersey rules, the most of that payment that may go toward repaying the loan is:
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-30.5 limits loan repayment to the outstanding loan times the percentage accelerated. Twenty-five percent of $40,000 is $10,000, so at least $40,000 goes to the owner.

items.stem: An owner accelerates half of a policy's death benefit under the surrender approach. Absent any other formula in the policy, the premium on the remaining coverage is:
options: Unchanged, since the policy stays in force
Waived for the rest of the insured's life
Reduced in proportion to the coverage left in force
Raised to cover the insurer's early payment
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-30.5 requires the premium to be proportionately reduced to reflect the amount of insurance remaining in effect, and it may be reduced further by a stated formula or become paid-up.

items.stem: In testing whether a contract qualifies as life insurance for federal tax purposes, the maturity date (including the date an endowment is payable) is deemed to be no earlier than the insured's age:
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 7702 deems the maturity date, including the date an endowment benefit is payable, to be no earlier than age 95 and no later than age 100. This is why short-term endowments generally cannot qualify as life insurance.

items.stem: When testing a contract under the federal definition of life insurance, any endowment benefit is deemed not to exceed:
options: The total of all premiums paid in
The cash surrender value at age 65
Twice the face amount at issue
The smallest death benefit the contract ever pays
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 7702 deems the amount of any endowment benefit not to exceed the least amount payable as a death benefit at any time under the contract.

items.stem: To qualify as life insurance under federal tax law, a contract must meet either the cash value accumulation test or:
options: The seven-pay test for modified endowments
Guideline premium limits plus the cash value corridor
The five-year Roth IRA holding period
The two-year incontestability period
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 7702 defines a life insurance contract as one that meets the cash value accumulation test, or meets the guideline premium requirements and falls within the cash value corridor. The seven-pay test is the modified endowment contract test, not part of this definition.

items.stem: A contract sold as life insurance is found to fail the federal definition of a life insurance contract. How is the growth inside the contract taxed to the policyholder?
options: As ordinary income, deferred until surrender
As long-term capital gain at surrender
Not at all while premiums continue
As ordinary income, year by year
items.explanation: 26 U.S.C. § 7702 treats the income on a contract that fails the definition of life insurance as ordinary income received or accrued by the policyholder each year.

items.stem: Under New Jersey's insurance code, a contract that pays an endowment benefit if the insured survives to a stated age is classified as:
options: Life insurance
An annuity
Health insurance
A security
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:17-3 provides that life insurance includes the granting of endowment benefits.

items.stem: A person with no New Jersey license or authorization collects premium payments from New Jersey residents on behalf of an out-of-state insurer, but never solicits or sells a policy. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Allowed, since he did not solicit or sell
Allowed, if the insurer is licensed in its home state
Prohibited, since receiving premiums is transacting insurance
Prohibited only if the policies are life policies
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:17-13(a)-(b) bars anyone, unless specifically authorized, from soliciting, negotiating, delivering a policy, receiving any premium, or otherwise transacting insurance in New Jersey.

items.stem: Every insurer transacting business in New Jersey must file its sworn annual financial statement with the commissioner by:
options: January 31
March 1
April 15
June 30
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:21-1(a) requires the annual statement, showing condition as of December 31, to be filed on or before March 1. Quarterly statements are due within 45 days after each quarter.

items.stem: An insurer incorporated under New Jersey law, with its home office in Newark, sells policies in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. In New Jersey it is a:
options: Foreign insurer
Alien insurer
Unauthorized insurer
Domestic insurer
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:17-7 defines a domestic insurer as one formed under the laws of this State.

items.stem: An insurer formed under Connecticut law is licensed to sell life insurance in New Jersey. In New Jersey it is a:
options: Foreign insurer
Domestic insurer
Alien insurer
Fraternal insurer
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:17-7 defines a foreign insurer as one formed under the laws of a U.S. jurisdiction other than New Jersey.

items.stem: An insurer formed under the laws of Canada has its U.S. office in New York and sells policies in New Jersey. In New Jersey it is a:
options: Domestic insurer
Foreign insurer
Alien insurer
Surplus lines insurer
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:17-7 defines an alien insurer as one formed under the laws of a country other than the United States, regardless of where its U.S. office is.

items.stem: Under New Jersey's definition of life insurance, an accidental death and dismemberment benefit attached to a life policy is treated as:
options: A health insurance coverage
A property and casualty coverage
An annuity benefit
Part of the life insurance
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:17-3 includes within life insurance provisions for additional benefits in event of death by accident or accidental means, or dismemberment or loss of sight.

items.stem: A contract promises periodic payments for life and also includes a small death benefit that is an incidental part of the contract. Under New Jersey law, the contract is classified as:
options: An annuity
Life insurance
Health insurance
A combination policy needing two filings
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:17-5 treats a contract with extra life or health benefits as an annuity if those benefits are a subsidiary or incidental part of the entire contract.

items.stem: In New Jersey, what does the commissioner issue to an insurer to show it may transact insurance in the state?
options: A producer license
A charter of incorporation
A certificate of authority
A surplus lines permit
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:17-12 defines a certificate of authority as the commissioner's certificate evidencing an insurer's authority to transact insurance in New Jersey. A license authorizes an agent, broker or solicitor.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, a person may sell, solicit or negotiate insurance in the state only if the person is:
options: Licensed for the line of authority involved
Licensed in any line of authority and appointed
Registered with the commissioner for that line
Supervised by a producer licensed for that line
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-29 bars anyone from selling, soliciting or negotiating insurance in New Jersey unless they are licensed for that line of authority. An appointment or employer does not replace the license.

items.stem: Maria holds a New Jersey producer license with only the property line of authority. A client asks her to arrange a life insurance policy. What does New Jersey law require before she can solicit the life policy?
options: A life line of authority on her license
Nothing, because a producer license covers all lines
Written consent from the client
A life insurer countersigning the application
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-29 requires a license for the specific line of authority being sold. A property-only producer must add the life line before soliciting life insurance.

items.stem: Which applicants for a New Jersey insurance producer license must pass a written examination?
options: Every applicant, including those licensed in another state
Resident individuals who are not exempt
Only applicants for the variable products line
Business entities applying for an agency license
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-31 requires resident individuals to pass a written examination unless they qualify for an exemption, such as prior licensing in another state.

items.stem: By law, the New Jersey producer examination must test an applicant's knowledge of each of the following EXCEPT:
options: The lines of authority applied for
The duties and responsibilities of a producer
New Jersey insurance laws and regulations
Securities sales practices under FINRA rules
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-31 lists three subjects: the lines of authority applied for, a producer's duties and responsibilities, and New Jersey insurance laws and regulations. FINRA securities rules are not among them.

items.stem: An applicant pays the New Jersey examination fee and then fails the exam. What happens to the fee?
options: It is not refunded
It is refunded in full
It is credited toward one retake
It is refunded minus an administrative charge
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-31 makes the examination fee nonrefundable, so failing the exam does not return any part of it.

items.stem: An applicant does not show up for a scheduled New Jersey licensing exam. To be rescheduled, the applicant must:
options: Wait 30 days and send a written rescheduling request
Submit a new application with the full fees and forms
Pay only a rescheduling fee, since the application stays on file
Request a waiver of the examination from the commissioner
items.explanation: Under N.J.S.A. 17:22A-31, an applicant who fails to appear or fails the exam may reapply, but must remit all required fees and forms before being rescheduled.

items.stem: In which languages must New Jersey offer the producer examination and its registration materials?
options: English only
English, Spanish and Portuguese
Any language the applicant requests
English and Spanish
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-31 requires the commissioner to offer the examination and registration materials in English and Spanish.

items.stem: What is the minimum age to be approved for a New Jersey resident insurance producer license?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-32 requires the commissioner to find that a resident individual applicant is at least 18 years of age.

items.stem: Jordan applies for a New Jersey resident producer license two months before his 18th birthday. When can the commissioner approve the license?
options: Immediately, since he passed the exam
Once he turns 18
Once he turns 21
Only with a parent's written consent
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-32 requires the commissioner to find that a resident individual applicant is at least 18 years of age before approving the license.

items.stem: Before approving a resident individual's application for the life line, the commissioner must find that the applicant has:
options: Completed a prelicensing course in any line within five years
Served an apprenticeship with a licensed life producer
Obtained a life insurer appointment before applying
Completed a prelicensing course for the life line
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-32 requires completion of a prelicensing course of study for the lines of authority applied for. Work experience, an appointment and a degree are not required.

items.stem: A corporation wants a New Jersey producer license so it can act as an insurance agency. Besides paying the fees, what must it do?
options: Designate a licensed producer to sign every policy it sells
Designate a licensed producer responsible for its compliance
Have each officer licensed for every line the entity sells
Post a compliance bond with the commissioner
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-32 requires a business entity to pay the fees and designate a licensed producer, or producers, responsible for its compliance with New Jersey insurance law.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, who bears the cost of the criminal history background check required of a producer license applicant?
options: The applicant's prospective employer
The Department of Banking and Insurance
The applicant's appointing insurer
The applicant personally
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-32 states that the applicant bears the cost of the criminal history record background check, including processing costs.

items.stem: Which of the following must an applicant for a New Jersey resident producer license submit to the commissioner?
options: Fingerprints and consent to a criminal background check
Fingerprints and a certified copy of a credit report
Written consent to a background check by the appointing insurer
A notarized affidavit of good moral character
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-32 requires the applicant's name, address, fingerprints and written consent for a criminal history record background check.

items.stem: Under New Jersey's lines of authority, the life line includes coverage on human lives along with benefits of:
options: Medical expense coverage for sickness
Endowments and annuities
Long-term care coverage
Property and casualty coverage for families
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 defines the life line as coverage on human lives, including benefits of endowment and annuities.

items.stem: A producer licensed only for the life line wants to sell a universal life policy whose cash value is invested in market-linked subaccounts. Which additional line of authority must be on her New Jersey license?
options: Accident and health or sickness
An annuity products line
Credit
Variable life and variable annuity products
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 lists variable life and variable annuity products, meaning products that reflect a separate account's investment experience, as their own line of authority, separate from the life line.

items.stem: The personal lines line of authority covers:
options: Noncommercial property and casualty coverage for families
Life and health coverage sold to individuals
Commercial property coverage for small businesses
Credit insurance sold with consumer loans
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 defines personal lines as property and casualty coverage sold to individuals and families for primarily noncommercial purposes.

items.stem: A resident individual's New Jersey producer license stays in effect, unless revoked or suspended, as long as the producer:
options: Keeps at least one active insurer appointment
Pays the fee on time and meets education requirements
Retakes the licensing exam every four years
Writes a minimum amount of new business each year
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 keeps a license in effect as long as the fee is timely paid and, for resident individuals, education requirements are timely satisfied.

items.stem: A producer lets her license lapse by missing the renewal fee. Within what period after the due date may she reinstate the same license without retaking the exam?
options: 30 days
90 days
6 months
12 months
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 allows reinstatement of a lapsed license within 12 months from the renewal fee due date without passing a written examination.

items.stem: A producer's license renewal fee was due June 30. She does not pay it until May 15 of the following year. What is the result?
options: She must retake the licensing exam
Her license is reinstated with no penalty
She may reinstate without an exam but must pay a late penalty
She must wait 90 days and then reapply
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 allows a lapsed license to be reinstated within 12 months of the renewal fee due date without a written exam, but a penalty of up to double the unpaid renewal fee is required for a late fee.

items.stem: When a New Jersey renewal fee is received after the due date, the penalty may be up to:
options: The amount of the unpaid renewal fee
Triple the unpaid renewal fee
Double the unpaid renewal fee
A flat $500
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 sets the late renewal penalty at an amount not to exceed double the unpaid renewal fee.

items.stem: A producer deployed on military service cannot complete license renewal on time. What may the producer do?
options: Request an extension from the testing vendor
Have a designee renew the license for the producer
Renew only after retaking the examination
Ask the commissioner to waive the renewal procedures
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 lets a producer who cannot renew because of military service or another extenuating circumstance request a waiver of renewal procedures.

items.stem: Within how many days must a New Jersey licensee inform the commissioner of a change of address?
options: 10 days
15 days
30 days
60 days
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 requires licensees to inform the commissioner of a change of address within 30 days of the change.

items.stem: Darnell, a licensed producer, moves to a new apartment in Newark on March 1. When must he tell the commissioner his new address?
options: Within 30 days of the move
At his next license renewal
Within 90 days of the move
Only if his business address also changes
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-33 requires notice of a change of address within 30 days of the change, not at renewal.

items.stem: A Pennsylvania resident wants a New Jersey nonresident producer license. Which of the following is a requirement?
options: Being licensed in Pennsylvania for at least two years
Holding a Pennsylvania resident license in good standing
Holding a resident license in any state, active or lapsed
Being licensed in Pennsylvania and passing New Jersey's law exam
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-34 grants a nonresident license to a person currently licensed as a resident producer in good standing in the home state, without a New Jersey exam or course.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for a New Jersey nonresident producer license?
options: A resident license in good standing in the home state
A home state that licenses New Jersey residents on the same basis
Payment of the required licensing fees
Passing New Jersey's producer licensing examination
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-34 grants a nonresident license to a producer in good standing in a home state that licenses New Jersey residents on the same basis, who files the application and pays the fees. No New Jersey exam is required.

items.stem: One condition for New Jersey to grant a nonresident producer license is that the applicant's home state:
options: Grants resident licenses to New Jersey residents who move there
Grants nonresident licenses only to producers who pass its exam
Grants nonresident licenses to New Jersey residents on the same basis
Charges the same license fees as New Jersey
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-34 requires that the applicant's home state award nonresident licenses to New Jersey residents on the same basis, which is reciprocity.

items.stem: By applying for and receiving a New Jersey nonresident license, the producer is deemed to have appointed whom as agent to receive service of legal process in New Jersey?
options: The insurer that appointed the producer
A registered agent the producer designates in New Jersey
The producer's home state insurance regulator
The New Jersey commissioner
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-34 provides that a nonresident licensee is deemed to have appointed the commissioner as agent to receive service of original legal process in New Jersey.

items.stem: A New Jersey resident producer moves to Delaware and wants to keep a New Jersey license. What must the producer do within 30 days of the move?
options: File a change of address and certification from Delaware
Surrender the license and reapply with a new fee
Pass the Delaware exam and send the score to New Jersey
Nothing until the next renewal date
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-34 requires a resident producer who moves out of New Jersey to file a change of address and certification from the new resident state within 30 days. No fee or new application is required.

items.stem: A producer's Ohio license, held in good standing, was cancelled when he left the business. To skip New Jersey's prelicensing education and exam for the same lines, his application must be received within how many days of the cancellation?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-35 exempts a previously licensed producer from prelicensing education and the exam if the application is received within 90 days of the prior license's cancellation and good standing is certified.

items.stem: A licensed Florida producer moves to New Jersey. Within how many days of establishing legal residence must she apply to become a New Jersey resident licensee?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-35 requires a producer who moves to New Jersey to apply for a resident license within 90 days of establishing legal residence.

items.stem: A producer licensed for life and health in Florida moves to New Jersey and applies on time. Ordinarily, what is required to obtain the same lines in New Jersey?
options: Both prelicensing education and the exam
Neither prelicensing education nor the exam
The exam only
Prelicensing education only
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-35 requires no prelicensing education or examination for lines already held in the prior state, unless the commissioner provides otherwise by regulation.

items.stem: A producer wants to do business as "Garden State Coverage" instead of under her legal name. When must she notify the commissioner?
options: Within 30 days after first using it
When she files her next license renewal
Before she begins using the name
Within 10 days after registering it with the county
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-36 requires a producer to notify the commissioner prior to using an assumed name.

items.stem: A temporary producer license issued in New Jersey may last no longer than:
options: 30 days
90 days
180 days
12 months
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-37 limits a temporary producer license, issued without an exam, to a period not to exceed 180 days.

items.stem: The commissioner issues a temporary producer license to a deceased producer's spouse on March 1. Absent a new license, the latest it can remain in effect is about:
options: March 31
June 1
August 28
March 1 of the next year
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-37 limits a temporary license to a period not to exceed 180 days. 180 days after March 1 is about August 28.

items.stem: A licensed producer dies suddenly. To allow time to sell the business, the commissioner may issue a temporary license under the death or disability provision to:
options: The spouse or court-appointed representative
The producer's appointing insurer
A licensed producer the clients choose
The agency's largest client
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-37 allows a temporary license for the surviving spouse or court-appointed personal representative of a producer who dies or becomes disabled.

items.stem: A producer is entering active service in the U.S. armed forces. Under the temporary license provision written for that situation, the commissioner may issue a temporary license to:
options: A designee the producer names
The producer's appointing insurer
The producer's clients, acting jointly
An unlicensed employee, with no limits on authority
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-37 allows a temporary license for the designee of a producer entering active service in the U.S. armed forces.

items.stem: When the commissioner requires a temporary licensee to have a sponsor, who may serve as the sponsor?
options: A suitable family member who assumes responsibility
A licensed producer or insurer that assumes responsibility
A licensed attorney who assumes responsibility
A bonded surety that assumes responsibility
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-37 lets the commissioner require a suitable sponsor who is a licensed producer or insurer and assumes responsibility for all acts of the temporary licensee.

items.stem: During the licensing exam, a candidate is caught using notes hidden in a jacket. Under New Jersey law, this conduct is:
options: A reason to fail the current attempt, and nothing more
A ground for the commissioner to refuse the license
Permitted if the notes came from an approved course
A matter for the testing vendor alone
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-40 lists improperly using notes or other reference material to complete the licensing exam as a cause to refuse, suspend or revoke a license.

items.stem: New Jersey's licensing law lists conviction of which of the following as a ground to refuse, suspend or revoke a producer license?
options: A crime of the first degree only
A crime of the first or second degree only
Any disorderly persons offense
A felony or crime of the fourth degree or higher
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-40 lists conviction of a felony or crime of the fourth degree or higher as a cause for license action. It is not limited to insurance crimes or recent convictions.

items.stem: A producer ignores a court order requiring child support payments. Can this affect the producer's license?
options: No, because family law matters are unrelated to licensing
Yes, but just when a client also complains
No, unless the producer also misses a premium payment
Yes, it is a listed ground for action against the license
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-40 lists failing to comply with an administrative or court order imposing a child support obligation as a cause for license action.

items.stem: A New Jersey producer is indicted. Failing to notify the commissioner within how many days of the indictment is a ground for action against the license?
options: 10 days
30 days
60 days
90 days
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-40 makes failing to notify the commissioner within 30 days of a conviction, indictment or the filing of formal criminal charges a cause for license action.

items.stem: The commissioner denies an application for a producer license. What is the applicant entitled to?
options: A written reason, and a review by a producer licensing board
A written reason, and a hearing if demanded in writing
A hearing, and a refund of the application fee
A hearing, and a temporary license until it ends
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-40 requires the commissioner to state the reason for a denial or nonrenewal in writing, and lets the applicant make a written demand for a hearing.

items.stem: An agency's managers knew one of their producers was misappropriating premiums but neither reported it nor took corrective action. What can happen to the agency's own license?
options: Nothing, since only the individual producer is responsible
It transfers automatically to another manager
It may be suspended, revoked or refused after a hearing
Nothing, because the entity holds a separate license
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-40 allows a business entity's license to be suspended, revoked or refused, after a hearing, when its partners, officers or managers knew or should have known of a violation and neither reported nor corrected it.

items.stem: A producer under investigation surrenders his license, hoping to avoid discipline. What is the effect on the commissioner's authority?
options: The commissioner may still impose penalties
The investigation has to end
Authority passes to the appointing insurer
A court takes over the matter
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-40 preserves the commissioner's authority to enforce the law and impose penalties even if the license was surrendered or lapsed.

items.stem: A licensed producer wants to split a commission with an unlicensed friend who solicited the client and negotiated the life policy. Under New Jersey law, this payment is:
options: Prohibited
Allowed if disclosed to the client
Allowed up to 10% of the commission
Allowed if the insurer approves it
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-41 bars an insurer or producer from paying a commission to someone for selling, soliciting or negotiating insurance if that person must be licensed and is not.

items.stem: A retired producer no longer holds a license, but was licensed when she sold several policies. May she receive renewal commissions on those policies?
options: No, because commissions stop when the license ends
Yes, because she was licensed at the time of the sale
No, unless she reinstates her license
Yes, but just for 12 months after she retires
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-41 allows renewal or deferred commissions to be paid to a person who was properly licensed at the time of the sale.

items.stem: A New Jersey producer is fined in an administrative action by the New York insurance department. When must the producer report it to the New Jersey commissioner?
options: Within 10 days of the hearing
Within 60 days of paying the fine
Within 30 days of the final disposition
Only at the next license renewal
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-47 requires a producer to report administrative action taken in another jurisdiction within 30 days of the final disposition, with a copy of the order.

items.stem: A New Jersey producer is being criminally prosecuted. The producer's report to the commissioner must include:
options: A letter from the producer's attorney and a bail receipt
A statement from the appointing insurer and the arrest report
A character reference and proof of current employment
The initial complaint and the order from the pretrial hearing
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-47 requires a producer reporting a criminal prosecution to include a copy of the initial complaint filed, the order resulting from the hearing and any other relevant legal documents.

items.stem: A licensed agency pays a flat referral fee, owed whether or not a sale occurs, to an unlicensed real estate agent who only passes along a client's name and never discusses coverage. Under New Jersey's licensing law, this payment is:
options: Permitted, since she only referred the client
Prohibited, since the real estate agent is unlicensed
Permitted only if she becomes licensed within 90 days
Prohibited unless the commissioner approves it in advance
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:22A-41 lets an insurer or producer pay persons who do not sell, solicit or negotiate insurance, unless the payment would violate another law, such as the rebating rules.

items.stem: A producer tells a policyholder that her whole life policy's cash value will be forfeited next year unless she surrenders it now. The statement is false, and the producer is not offering her another policy. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Misrepresentation
Twisting
Churning
False advertising
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 prohibits misrepresentations made to a policyholder to induce a lapse, forfeiture or surrender. Lying about the policy's terms to get her to surrender is misrepresentation.

items.stem: An agency's website and brochures tell the public it "won the state's top customer service award five years running." No such award exists. Which unfair trade practice is this?
options: Defamation
Misrepresentation of policy terms
Unfair discrimination
False information and advertising
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 prohibits any advertisement or statement about the business of insurance that is untrue, deceptive or misleading, in any medium including radio.

items.stem: A producer tells prospects that a competing insurer "is about to be taken over by regulators," which is untrue, to steer new business away from that insurer. Which practice is this?
options: Defamation
Twisting
Rebating
Boycott
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 defines defamation as a false or maliciously critical statement about an insurer's financial condition that is calculated to injure a person in the insurance business.

items.stem: Several insurers agree among themselves to stop writing business through any agency that also places business with a new competitor, so the competitor cannot get established. This is an example of:
options: Unfair discrimination
Twisting
Defamation
Boycott, coercion and intimidation
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 prohibits concerted acts of boycott, coercion or intimidation that unreasonably restrain, or create a monopoly in, the business of insurance.

items.stem: Two applicants have the same age, health and risk class, with equal life expectancy. The underwriter charges one of them a higher life insurance rate because of the neighborhood he lives in. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Unfair discrimination
Permitted underwriting judgment
Rebating
A permitted territorial rating
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 prohibits unfair discrimination in life insurance rates between individuals of the same class and equal expectation of life.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the characteristics listed in New Jersey's ban on discrimination in issuing, withholding, extending or renewing a policy?
options: Creed
Ancestry
Occupation
National origin
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 bans discrimination because of race, creed, color, national origin or ancestry. Occupation is a legitimate underwriting factor and is not on the list.

items.stem: To close a life insurance sale, a producer offers to pay the client's first month's premium out of his own pocket. This is:
options: Rebating
Twisting
Permitted if disclosed in writing
Allowed as a marketing expense
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 prohibits paying any rebate of premium or other valuable consideration not specified in the contract as an inducement to buy insurance. Paying the client's premium is a rebate.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT treated as a rebate or unfair discrimination under New Jersey law?
options: Fair bonuses paid out of nonparticipating surplus
Fair bonuses out of surplus for policyholders who buy more
Premium reductions promised verbally but not in the contract
Insurer stock given to every new policyholder
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 excludes from rebating and discrimination the payment of fair and equitable bonuses or premium abatements to life policyholders out of surplus from nonparticipating insurance.

items.stem: At the end of a policy year, a group life insurer readjusts the group's premium rate based on the group's loss experience. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: An illegal rebate to the group
Unfair discrimination against other groups
Permitted, retroactive only for that policy year
Permitted, retroactive for up to three prior years
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 treats a group premium readjustment based on loss or expense experience as neither a rebate nor discrimination, and allows it to be retroactive only for that policy year.

items.stem: Under New Jersey's unfair trade practices law, improper claim handling by an insurer is an unfair claim settlement practice when it is committed:
options: Even once, against any single claimant
With enough frequency to affect ten or more claimants
Only in ways the commissioner has published in advance
Often enough to indicate a general business practice
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 defines unfair claim settlement practices as listed acts committed with such frequency as to indicate a general business practice.

items.stem: An insurer routinely sends claim payments to beneficiaries without saying which coverage each payment falls under. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Acceptable if the amount paid is correct
An unfair claim settlement practice
Required to protect beneficiary privacy
A violation only for health insurance claims
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 lists making claim payments without a statement of the coverage under which they are made as an unfair claim settlement practice.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, an insurer must keep a complete record of all complaints it has received since:
options: The start of the current calendar year
The date it was first licensed
Its most recent examination
The date five years before the current one
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 requires a complete record of all complaints received since the date of the last examination, including their number, line, nature, disposition and processing time.

items.stem: For New Jersey's complaint record requirement, a "complaint" is defined as:
options: Any oral or written expression of dissatisfaction
Any grievance filed with the Department of Banking and Insurance
Any written request for policy information
A grievance expressed in writing
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 defines a complaint, for the record-keeping requirement, as any written communication primarily expressing a grievance.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, an insurer's complaint record must show each of the following EXCEPT:
options: The nature of each complaint
How each complaint was resolved
The processing time for each complaint
The selling producer's name
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:29B-4 requires the complaint record to show the total number of complaints, their classification by line of insurance, and the nature, disposition and processing time of each. The selling producer is not a required element.

items.stem: An insurer charges a slightly lower premium to policyholders who pay by monthly payroll deduction. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Allowed, if the lower rate reflects the savings from the plan
An illegal rebate
Unfair discrimination between policyholders of the same class
Allowed, if the agent's commission is reduced by the same amount
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-14 allows lower rates on payroll deduction and similar plans when the rate is reasonably related to the savings made by using the plan.

items.stem: A producer offers a prospect a $200 gift card if she buys a life policy. She declines and never applies. Under New Jersey rules:
options: A violation, since the offer alone breaks the rule
No violation, since no policy was sold
A violation, but just if she had applied
No violation, if the gift card is worth under $25
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-2.3(a)-(e) bars offering an inducement not plainly expressed in the contract, and applies whether or not a contract of insurance is ultimately effected.

items.stem: A producer shows a client a comparison that leaves out her existing whole life policy's cash value, to persuade her to surrender it and buy a new policy from another insurer. This practice is called:
options: Rebating
Sliding
Churning
Twisting
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-2.8, titled "Twisting" prohibited, bars misleading representations or incomplete or fraudulent comparisons of policies or insurers made to induce a person to lapse, surrender or replace a policy.

items.stem: To win a replacement sale, a New Jersey insurer's new life policy offers to credit the client with the surrender charge she will pay on her old policy from another company. Under New Jersey rules, this is:
options: Not allowed, even if fully disclosed
Allowed, as a bonus to the client
Allowed, if disclosed on the replacement notice
Not allowed, unless the old insurer consents
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-48.7 bars a policy from providing credits for a surrender charge imposed under another contract, because such credits unfairly discriminate among contractholders based on the source of funding.

items.stem: A person commits four separate violations of New Jersey's Insurance Fraud Prevention Act. What is the maximum total civil penalty in a court action by the commissioner?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:33A-5(b) sets civil penalties of up to $5,000 for the first violation, $10,000 for the second and $15,000 for each subsequent violation: $5,000 + $10,000 + $15,000 + $15,000 = $45,000.

items.stem: A New Jersey producer comes to believe that a client submitted a fraudulent claim. Under the Insurance Fraud Prevention Act, whom must be notified?
options: The bureau and the Office of the Insurance Fraud Prosecutor
The insurer's special investigations unit, and no one else
The commissioner, at the producer's next license renewal
The county prosecutor in the client's home county
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17:33A-9(a)(1),(b) requires anyone who believes a violation occurred to notify the bureau and the Office of the Insurance Fraud Prosecutor immediately after discovery.

items.stem: Membership in the New Jersey Life and Health Insurance Guaranty Association is:
options: Voluntary for insurers with strong financial ratings
A condition of an insurer's authority to do business in New Jersey
Required only of insurers that sell annuities
Required only of mutual insurers
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-5 requires all member insurers to be and remain members of the association as a condition of their authority or license to transact insurance in New Jersey.

items.stem: After an insurer stops holding its New Jersey certificate of authority, it remains a member of the life and health guaranty association for:
options: 1 year
2 years
4 years
10 years
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-5 keeps an insurer a member for four years after it ceases to hold a certificate of authority or license.

items.stem: For administration and assessment, New Jersey's guaranty association for life and health insurers maintains which two accounts?
options: A life insurance and annuity account, and a health account
A life account and a separate annuity account
A health account and a separate long-term care account
A life and health account, and an unallocated annuity account
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-5 requires two accounts: the life insurance and annuity account (with life, annuity and unallocated annuity subaccounts) and the health account.

items.stem: An insured's life insurer becomes insolvent. Regardless of how many policies are involved, the guaranty association's limit for life insurance death benefits on one life is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-3(e) limits life insurance death benefits to $500,000 with respect to one life, regardless of the number of policies or contracts.

items.stem: John has two policies on his life with the same insurer, with death benefits of $300,000 and $350,000. The insurer becomes insolvent. The guaranty association's maximum obligation for John's death benefits is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-3(e) limits life insurance death benefits to $500,000 with respect to one life, regardless of the number of policies.

items.stem: When a life insurer fails, the guaranty association's limit on a life policy's net cash surrender and withdrawal values, for one life, is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-3(e) caps net cash surrender and net cash withdrawal values for life insurance at $100,000 with respect to one life.

items.stem: For annuities, the guaranty association's limit on net cash surrender and withdrawal values for one life is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-3(e) caps net cash surrender and net cash withdrawal values for annuity benefits at $250,000 with respect to one life.

items.stem: Maria has a $400,000 policy on her own life and an annuity with a $300,000 present value, both with the same insurer, which becomes insolvent. What is the most the guaranty association can be obligated to pay in total on these benefits for her?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-3(e) sets a $500,000 aggregate cap for any one individual across life insurance death benefits and annuity benefits, so $700,000 of combined benefits is limited to $500,000.

items.stem: The guaranty association's benefit limit for any one unallocated annuity contract is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-3(e) limits benefits for any one unallocated annuity contract to $2,000,000.

items.stem: Under New Jersey's Life and Health Insurance Guaranty Association Act, the limit on benefits for an accident or health insurance policy is:
options: Unlimited
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-3(e) provides unlimited benefits with respect to any one group, blanket or individual accident or health insurance policy. This is broader than the dollar caps many other states use.

items.stem: A producer tells a hesitant client, "Don't worry about this insurer's finances, because the state guaranty association will cover you anyway." Under New Jersey law, this statement is:
options: Acceptable, because the association does exist
Required disclosure at the point of sale
Acceptable if the coverage limits are also stated
Prohibited use of the association to induce a purchase
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-17 prohibits any producer or insurer from using the existence of the guaranty association, in any written or oral statement, for sales, solicitation or inducement to purchase.

items.stem: When must a member insurer give the policyowner the guaranty association's summary document?
options: Within 30 days after the policy is delivered
Only once the policyowner asks for it
After the insurer becomes impaired
No later than the day the policy is handed over
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-17 bars a member insurer from delivering a covered policy unless the summary document is delivered prior to or at the time of policy delivery.

items.stem: The disclaimer on the guaranty association's summary document must warn that any available coverage is conditioned on:
options: Payment of an annual guaranty fee
Continued residence in New Jersey
The policy being in force for two years
The insured's good health at the time of insolvency
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:32A-17 requires the disclaimer to warn that the association may not cover the policy, and that any coverage is subject to substantial limitations and conditioned on continued residence in New Jersey.

items.stem: New Jersey rules describe the capacity in which an insurance producer acts in conducting insurance business as:
options: Independent contractor
Agent of the commissioner
Guarantor of the insurer
Fiduciary
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-4.10 provides that an insurance producer acts in a fiduciary capacity in the conduct of his or her insurance business.

items.stem: Absent a different term in the producer's contract with the insurer or another controlling rule, a New Jersey producer must remit premium funds to the insurer within:
options: 2 business days
5 business days
10 calendar days
30 calendar days
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17C-2.2(a)-(b) requires premium funds to be remitted within five business days after receipt, unless the producer's contract, a written agreement, a statute or rule, or residual market rules provide otherwise.

items.stem: An insurer sends a producer a $400 return premium owed to a client after a policy change. Under New Jersey rules, the producer must pay or credit it to the client within:
options: 10 calendar days after receiving it
30 days after the policy change
5 business days after receiving it
The client's next renewal date
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17C-2.2(a)-(b) requires premiums due the insured to be paid or credited within five business days after the producer receives them.

items.stem: A New Jersey producer receives a new policy from the insurer for delivery. Unless the insured agrees in writing to a longer period, the producer must deliver or mail it within:
options: 5 calendar days
10 calendar days
15 calendar days
30 calendar days
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-4.6 requires delivery or mailing within 10 calendar days of the producer's receipt, unless the insured agrees in writing that the producer may keep it longer.

items.stem: A producer completes a life application with a client over the phone, then mails it to the client, who signs it at home and mails it back. Under New Jersey rules, is the producer required to witness the signature?
options: Yes, a producer witnesses all signatures on his applications
Yes, unless the client already owns a policy with the insurer
No, since witnessing is required for annuities and not life
No, since this one was not completed face to face
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-4.2 requires the producer to witness the signature only when the application is signed after being completed in a face-to-face meeting, and the insurer may waive this by prior written authorization.

items.stem: A client calls her New Jersey producer to change a policy, and the change is made. Within how many days must the producer confirm to her in writing the information she gave and that it was sent to the insurer?
options: 3 days
5 days
10 days
30 days
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-4.3(a) requires written notice within 10 days after a transaction that modifies an existing contract or application, confirming the information submitted and that it was sent to the insurer.

items.stem: In New Jersey, credit life insurance insures the life of:
options: The lender, against the borrower's default
The collateral that secures the loan
The borrower on a particular loan
The borrower's income while disabled
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:29-2 defines credit life insurance as insurance on the life of a debtor in connection with a specific loan or other credit transaction.

items.stem: Under New Jersey law, credit life insurance may be written on which plan?
options: Whole life
Universal life
Endowment
Term
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:29-3 allows credit life insurance only on the term plan, whether as individual policies to debtors or group policies issued to creditors.

items.stem: A borrower signs a car loan with $24,000 repayable in equal monthly installments. He has fallen behind, so his scheduled unpaid balance is $15,000 but his actual unpaid balance is $16,200. Under New Jersey law, the most credit life insurance that may be in force now is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:29-4(a)(1) caps credit life on installment debt at the scheduled or actual unpaid indebtedness, whichever is greater. Here that is the actual balance of $16,200.

items.stem: Unless extended at no added cost to the debtor, New Jersey credit life coverage may last no more than how long past the loan's scheduled maturity date?
options: 15 days
30 days
60 days
6 months
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:29-5 bars the term of credit insurance from extending more than 15 days beyond the scheduled maturity date, except when extended without additional cost to the debtor.

items.stem: A debtor dies owing $8,000 on a loan, and the credit life benefit payable is $10,000. Under New Jersey law, how is the benefit paid?
options: $10,000 to the creditor, which refunds the excess to the debtor's estate
$8,000 to the creditor, and $2,000 to the debtor's named beneficiary or estate
$10,000 to the debtor's named beneficiary, who then pays the creditor
$8,000 to the creditor, and $2,000 to the co-signer on the loan
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:29-6(b) requires benefits to be paid to the creditor to reduce or extinguish the unpaid debt, with any excess payable to a beneficiary other than the creditor named by the debtor, or to the debtor's estate.

items.stem: An insurer's premium for a borrower's credit life coverage is $300, and the lender adds $50 on top as a service charge for the coverage. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Allowed, since lenders may mark up credit insurance
Allowed, if the markup is disclosed in writing
Not allowed, unless the loan is over $25,000
Not allowed, since the debtor's charge may not exceed the insurer's premium
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:29-8(b)-(d) bars charging a debtor more for credit life or credit health insurance than the premiums charged by the insurer.

items.stem: A New Jersey group life policy must give the policyholder a grace period of how many days for premiums after the first?
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:27-72(b)-(c) requires a 31-day grace period for premiums after the first, during which death benefit coverage continues.

items.stem: A New Jersey group life policy's validity may not be contested, except for nonpayment of premiums, once it has been in force for:
options: 1 year
2 years
3 years
5 years
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:27-72(b)-(c) bars contesting the group policy's validity, except for nonpayment of premiums, after it has been in force for two years from issue.

items.stem: An employee leaves her job and loses her group life coverage. To convert to an individual policy without evidence of insurability, she must apply and pay the first premium within:
options: 15 days
31 days
60 days
90 days
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:27-72(i) allows conversion without evidence of insurability if the application is made and the first premium paid within 31 days after termination.

items.stem: When a former employee, Dana, converts group life coverage to an individual policy, the premium is based on:
options: The age Dana has reached when the individual policy takes effect
The age at which Dana first joined the group plan
The average age of the group's members
A flat conversion rate set by the commissioner
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:27-72(i)(3) sets the converted policy's premium at the insurer's customary rate for the form, amount, risk class and the age attained on the individual policy's effective date.

items.stem: An employee with $150,000 of group life coverage leaves his job and has no other group coverage. Without evidence of insurability, the most he can convert to an individual policy is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:27-72(i)(2) limits the converted policy to the amount of life insurance that ceased because of termination, less any new group coverage within 31 days.

items.stem: A former employee was never told of her group life conversion right before the conversion period ended. She finally receives notice 20 days after that period ended. Under New Jersey law, how long does she now have to convert?
options: No time, since the period has already ended
15 days after she receives the notice
31 days after she receives the notice
60 days after she receives the notice
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:27-73 extends the conversion period to 15 days after notice when notice was not given at least 15 days before the period expired, but never beyond 60 days after the original deadline. Here that gives her 15 days from notice.

items.stem: A producer shows a client an incomplete comparison that hides the surrender charges on a new annuity, to persuade her to cash in her current annuity and buy the new one. This is known as:
options: Twisting
Rebating
Defamation
Sliding
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-6 prohibits misleading representations or incomplete or fraudulent comparisons of policies or annuities made to induce someone to surrender one and take out another. This is twisting.

items.stem: New Jersey's prohibition on misleading policy comparisons applies when the comparison is used to induce someone to do which of the following?
options: Increase the face amount of an existing policy
Change the payment mode of an existing policy
Keep or convert a current policy
Add a rider to an existing policy
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-6 covers misleading comparisons made to induce a person to lapse, forfeit, surrender, terminate, retain or convert a policy, not only to replace it.

items.stem: A producer persuades a client to drop her whole life policy and buy a new one from a different insurer, using a comparison that leaves out the new policy's surrender charges. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Rebating
Defamation
Twisting
A permitted replacement
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-6 prohibits incomplete or misleading comparisons made to induce someone to lapse or surrender a policy and take one out in another insurer. That is twisting.

items.stem: A producer tells a prospect that the participating policy he is selling "comes from a line of policies that has paid 8% dividends every year for 20 years." Similar policies actually paid between 3% and 5%. Under New Jersey law, the statement is:
options: Permitted, since dividends are not guaranteed
Misrepresentation
Permitted if an illustration is also provided
Twisting
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-3 prohibits false or misleading statements about dividends or surplus previously paid on similar policies.

items.stem: An insurer sells a 10-year term policy under the product name "Lifetime Wealth Builder." Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Misrepresentation of what the product is
Permitted, because product names are marketing
Twisting
Permitted if the policy form says it is term insurance
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-3 prohibits using any name or title of a policy or annuity that misrepresents its true nature.

items.stem: A producer offers to give a new life insurance client half of the producer's commission on the policy. Under New Jersey law, this is:
options: Commission splitting, which is legal between licensed persons
Permitted if the client signs a written waiver
An illegal rebate
A permitted marketing allowance
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-13 prohibits giving, as an inducement, any rebate of premiums or of any agent's, solicitor's or broker's commission on the contract.

items.stem: After a hearing, the commissioner finds a producer violated New Jersey's life and annuity trade practice rules without knowing, or having reason to know, it was a violation. The maximum penalty per violation is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-17 caps the penalty at $1,000 for each violation unless the person knew or reasonably should have known it was a violation.

items.stem: If a producer knew or reasonably should have known that the conduct violated New Jersey's life and annuity trade practice rules, the maximum penalty per violation is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-17 raises the maximum penalty to $5,000 for every violation when the person knew or reasonably should have known it was a violation.

items.stem: After a hearing, a producer is found to have knowingly made three misleading policy comparisons in violation of New Jersey's life trade practice rules. The maximum total penalty is:
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:30-17 allows up to $5,000 for every violation when the person knew or reasonably should have known it was a violation. Three violations come to $15,000.

items.stem: When the commissioner finds, after a hearing, that a person engaged in a prohibited life or annuity trade practice, the commissioner issues:
options: A desist warning with no penalty possible
An order to cease and desist
An automatic license revocation
A referral for criminal prosecution
